ref: #edit-termo
subject: Buscar
message: The text "Buscar" has at most 2.85:1 contrast with what is behind it (#999999 on #ffffff), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a pseudo-element). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input title="Buscar" data-drupal-selector="edit-termo" class="form-text form-control" type="text" id="edit-termo" name="termo" value="" size="60" placeholder="Do que você precisa hoje?">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The search field #edit-termo. No text 'Buscar' is rendered: that is its title, which is its accessible name. The pixels measured, #999999 on white at 14px and 2.85:1 (axeReason pseudoContent), are those of its placeholder 'Do que você precisa hoje?'. Bootstrap's '.form-control::placeholder{color:#999}' is in the live CSS, and the screenshot shows light grey italic text. So the sentence misnames the text. The field fails 1.4.3 all the same, because the placeholder is its only visible prompt (there is no visible label) and it has 2.85:1. The claim points at that defect, the low-contrast grey text in this field with the right colours and ratio, in imperfect words. It duplicates the placeholder finding on the same input.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The search input #edit-termo. 'Buscar' is only its title attribute (its accessible name): no text 'Buscar' is rendered, and the field is empty, so the sentence is not true as worded. The snapshot's 'text' measurement (883 pixels, #999999 on #ffffff, 2.85:1, 14px) is the same set of pixels as the placeholder 'Do que você precisa hoje?', whose CSS is .form-control::placeholder{color:#999} on a white field. Typed text would be #555 (7.46:1), so the only failing text is the placeholder, which Understanding 1.4.3 explicitly includes. The claim's measurement and colours point at that real defect in imperfect words (wrong quoted string, a duplicate of the placeholder finding), so in good faith it names the failure. The live page has the same input and CSS.

ref: #bloco-governo-digital > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > h2
subject: heading click
message: This element ("Serviços para você!") takes keyboard focus and listens to click, so it works as a control, but the browser exposes it as heading, with no control role: a screen reader does not announce it as a button or a link (F59). Use the native element (button, a) or give it the role of the control it is.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The h2 'Serviços para você!' has tabindex=0, and the site script binds a click on it ('#bloco-governo-digital .header-bloco-governo-digital h2').click(...toggleClass('show-mobile')). The capture holds as claimed: it is focusable, has a click listener and has the role heading. At 1280px the toggled class has no visible effect. At widths up to 575px, which means phones and also a 1280px desktop at 400% zoom, the live CSS hides the category buttons, gives the h2 a pointer cursor and a caret, and the click shows or hides them. There the h2 is a disclosure control exposed as a heading, with no button role and no expanded state: 4.1.2 fails (and it cannot be activated with Enter). The claim names that failure: it works as a control but is exposed as a heading with no control role.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The h2 'Serviços para você!' with tabindex=0. The tabindex alone is a site pattern (every h2 has it), but the live JS binds a click on this h2 that toggles 'show-mobile' on its header. The live CSS at max-width 575px hides the category buttons, gives the h2 cursor:pointer and a caret, and shows them on show-mobile, so on phones the heading is a disclosure toggle. At the captured 1280px width the click has no visible effect, which was my main doubt, but the same element in the same page works as a control for phone users and exposes only a heading role, with no button role and no expanded state. That fails 4.1.2 for the reason the claim names. The live page matches.

ref: #form-field-name
subject: Nome
message: The placeholder "Nome" has a contrast of 2.35:1 with the field (#70707099 on #ffffff). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input size="1" type="text" name="form_fields[name]" id="form-field-name" class="elementor-field elementor-size-sm  elementor-field-textual" placeholder="Nome">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Placeholder contrast: the 'Nome' field in the 'Dê o primeiro passo' lead form. The placeholder is its only visible label, because the label element is screen-reader-only. In the screenshot the placeholder renders as #a9a9a9 on the white field (computed rgba(112,112,112,.6) over #fff), which I measured from pixels at 2.35:1, matching the claim. Understanding 1.4.3 says the criterion applies to text 'including placeholder text'. G148 does not apply because the author sets the field's white background and text colour. The text is 15px at weight 500, so 4.5:1 is needed. The live page's CSS sets no placeholder colour, so users get the same default rendering. captureDiffers: no.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The 'Nome' text field of the 'Dê o primeiro passo na conquista do seu sonho' lead form, white field on a blue band. The placeholder style comes from Elementor's frontend.min.css (.elementor-field-textual::placeholder {color: inherit; opacity: .6}), so the grey text is the field colour #707070 at 60% opacity, about #A9A9A9 on the white field. I measured the screenshot: the darkest glyph pixel of the placeholder is #A9A9A9 on #FFFFFF, 2.35:1, matching the claim. The text is 15px weight 500, so it is not large text and needs 4.5:1. Looking for an exemption: the field is enabled, so the text is not incidental; Understanding 1.4.3 says the criterion applies to placeholder text; and the field's only label is visually hidden (elementor-screen-only), so this placeholder is the only visible label, which makes it informative text. No reason for a pass holds up. My own fetch of the live page (curl with a browser user agent, itself automated) returns the same markup for this element as the snapshot, so nothing found differs for this claim; the screenshot is taller than the snapshot's layout (the course grid grew after the tree was read), which does not touch it.

subject: for=form-field-email
message: 2 elements have id="form-field-email": this label names the first of them, not the field beside it. Give each field a unique id.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the screen-only label 'E-mail' (for=form-field-email) of the footer newsletter form. The page has two inputs with id=form-field-email, so this label resolves to the first one in the lead form, whose name becomes 'E-mail E-mail'. The claim is true of the capture, and the live HTML has the same duplicate. But 4.1.2 asks that the control have a programmatically determinable name. The footer field still has one: Chrome computes 'Digite seu e-mail' from its placeholder, and the ACT rule e086e5 (mapped to 4.1.2) accepts a placeholder as the accessible name (Passed Example 5). The lead-form field's doubled name 'E-mail E-mail' is redundant but still accurate. The duplicate id is a 4.1.1 parsing matter, which WCAG 2.1's note treats as always satisfied for HTML. So no control fails 4.1.2 here: the rule treats the broken reference itself as the failure, a stricter rule than the criterion's.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The visually hidden label 'E-mail' of the footer newsletter form has for="form-field-email". That id appears twice, on the lead form's e-mail field and on the footer field, so the label names the first one, as the claim says (that field's name becomes 'E-mail E-mail'). For 4.1.2, though, no component ends up without an accurate name and role. The footer field is still a textbox with the name 'Digite seu e-mail', from its placeholder (the snapshot's browser name), and the lead form's field keeps an accurate, if doubled, name. A label is not a user interface component itself. Duplicate ids as such were a 4.1.1 matter, which the 2023 errata treats as always satisfied for HTML. They fail 4.1.2 only when they leave a component with a missing or wrong name, which is not the case here. Because the label is screen-only, no visible relationship is lost either. The rule flags the broken reference as a failure in itself, which is stricter than the criterion. My own fetch of the live page (curl with a browser user agent, itself automated) returns the same markup for this element as the snapshot, so nothing found differs for this claim; the screenshot is taller than the snapshot's layout (the course grid grew after the tree was read), which does not touch it.

AGORA TEM"; its alt is "Slider 1". claimTrue yes: at capture the slide is inactive, off-screen (x beyond the 1280 viewport) and its wrapper has aria-hidden="true", and no text on the page gives the banner's message. The live page (fetched 2026-11-25) has the same Essential Blocks slider with the same seven images in the same order and settings autoplay true, autoplaySpeed 3000, infinite true; after hydration each image gets its slide title ("Slider N") as alt, as in the snapshot, so the capture matches what users receive (the full-page screenshot, taken a moment later, shows the carousel on slide 4, which is that rotation, not a different page). elementFails yes, but not for the claim's reason: the carousel sets aria-hidden only on inactive, off-screen slides and sets aria-hidden="false" on the current one (as the snapshot shows for slide 1), so when autoplay brings this slide in, the image is exposed with the alt "Slider 1", a placeholder that is not an equivalent of the banner's text (F30); hiding an off-screen slide is not the defect. The claim blames the aria-hidden state and says nothing about the alternative, so it points at something else: false_positive, the element failing 1.1.1 for its placeholder alt. Cause context_missing: the checker was not given the carousel state (inactive slick-slide, autoplay) that makes the hiding legitimate.

The element fails 1.1.1 for a reason the claim does not name: its alt is the placeholder "Slider 1" (F30), which is what a screen reader hears when the slide is shown. captureDiffers: the live HTML serves the same slides and settings. False positive.

ref: #mod-search-searchword
subject: Pesquisar...
message: The placeholder "Pesquisar..." has a contrast of 1.88:1 with the field (#a7a7a7 on #e2e2e2). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input aria-label="Pesquisar" name="searchword" id="mod-search-searchword" maxlength="200" class="inputbox search-query" type="text" size="0" placeholder="Pesquisar...">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header search field #mod-search-searchword (aria-label 'Pesquisar'), whose placeholder 'Pesquisar...' is the only visible text label next to the magnifier icon. template.css and legacy.css set the placeholder colour for input[type=text] to #999; the input's own background is none and it sits on '.search { background: #e2e2e2 }'. #999999 on #e2e2e2 is 2.20:1, far below 4.5:1 for 14px weight-300 text. Understanding 1.4.3 states that the criterion 'applies to text in the page, including placeholder text', so the field fails 1.4.3. The claim's #a7a7a7 and 1.88:1 are anti-aliased pixel values rather than the specified colour (the specified pair gives 2.20:1), so the sentence as worded does not hold exactly (claimTrue no), but it names the actual failure: placeholder text well under 4.5:1 against the field. skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the header search field #mod-search-searchword. Its placeholder 'Pesquisar...' is the only visible text label, next to a magnifier icon. template.css gives the input background:none inside .search {background:#e2e2e2 ...}, and the placeholder colour from legacy.css/template.css is #999. #999 on #e2e2e2 is 2.20:1, not the 1.88:1 (#a7a7a7) Rampa read from anti-aliased pixels, so the sentence's numbers are off (claimTrue no). The claim names the real failure, a placeholder contrast under 4.5:1.

ref: #form-field-email
message: The field "Email" asks for the user's email address but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="email" is missing.

patch.ref: #form-field-email
patch.before: <input size="1" type="email" name="form_fields[email]" id="form-field-email" class="elementor-field elementor-size-xs  elementor-field-textual" placeholder="Seu email.." required="required">
patch.after: <input size="1" type="email" name="form_fields[email]" id="form-field-email" class="elementor-field elementor-size-xs  elementor-field-textual" placeholder="Seu email.." required="required" autocomplete="email">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The input is the email field of the footer newsletter sign-up form ("Cadastro"). It asks for the user's own email address, and email is one of the input purposes listed in WCAG 2.1 section 7. In the capture and in the live HTML it has type="email" and a screen-reader label "Email", but no autocomplete attribute. type="email" gives the data type, not the input purpose, and the sufficient technique H98 needs autocomplete="email". Without it the purpose is not programmatically determinable, so 1.3.5 fails, as the claim says. The live markup is identical.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the footer newsletter sign-up field (input type="email", label "Email" hidden visually, placeholder "Seu email..") in the "Cadastro" form, which asks for the visitor's own email address. The captured HTML has no autocomplete attribute, and the live HTML is the same (no autocomplete anywhere on the page), so the claim is true and the capture does not differ. 1.3.5 applies: the field collects information about the user and "email" is in the Input Purposes list. I looked for a technique that would make it pass: type="email" only says the value is an email address, not that it is the user's own, and it is not the sufficient technique (H98, autocomplete); nothing else on the field identifies its purpose. So the element fails for the reason the claim gives.

subject: Início
message: The text "Início" has at most 3.95:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ffffff on #ff0137), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a pseudo-element). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the 'Início' link of the main navigation, the current page's item (li.current-menu-item). claimTrue: the snapshot's pixel measure records foreground #ffffff from CSS on a uniform #ff0137 background, 18px at weight 700, 3.954:1, with axe-core deferring because of pseudo content, exactly as the message says. elementFails: the live theme CSS (inline critical CSS and style.css) sets .header-navbar color #fff, the menu links to font-size 18px, font-weight 700 and color inherit, and .primary-menu>li.current-menu-item>a background #ff0137, a persistent state on the home page, not hover only; the screenshot's navbar shows white text on (255,1,55), and I compute 3.95:1. 18px bold is 13.5pt, under the 14pt bold (about 18.67px) large-text threshold, so 4.5:1 applies and the text fails 1.4.3 (the other menu items, white on #c81b23, reach 5.77:1). captureDiffers: the full-page screenshot draws the affixed (fixed-position) navbar near y=1836 instead of at its snapshot bounds y=130, a capture artefact of a sticky header that does not touch the colours or size; the live HTML and CSS fetched now match the capture. The claim names the real failure, so true_positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the 'Início' link in the desktop main menu. It is the current menu item on the home page (li.current-menu-item). claimTrue: I sampled the screenshot where the full-page capture drew the sticky navbar (about y=1838). The Início box is #ff0137 behind white glyphs (#ffffff), which gives 3.95:1. The neighbouring items sit on the bar's #c81b23 (5.77:1). elementFails: the live inline CSS and the theme's style.css both set '.site-navigation .primary-menu>li>a{font-size:18px;font-weight:700}' and '.primary-menu>li.current-menu-item>a{background:#ff0137}', with white text inherited from .header-navbar{color:#fff}. That background is the item's permanent current-page state, not only a hover or focus state. 18px bold is 13.5pt, under the 14pt bold that counts as large text, so the 4.5:1 minimum applies. I found no text-shadow, and the item is not incidental or a logotype. I looked for a reason it could pass and found none, so 3.95:1 fails 1.4.3. The stylesheet's display:none on .site-navigation applies only at max-width 991px, so the menu is visible at the 1280px viewport Rampa used. Below that width this menu is hidden and the off-canvas one takes its place. captureDiffers: the full-page capture shows the sticky navbar mid-page instead of under the logo (an affix artefact), but the colours, font size and active state in the capture match the live CSS fetched today. Nothing that bears on this claim differs. The claim names the real failure, so the label is true_positive.

patch.to: Logotipo do projeto O Digital Disfuncional

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the article's lead image, a non-linked figure with no caption, above the h1. The crop and the screenshot show the cover art of the newsletter: the words 'O Digital Disfuncional' in large white type over an abstract illustration of heads, eyes, arrows and documents marked with an X. Its alt is the article headline, which is word for word the h1 just below it. claimTrue: yes. The image does not show the headline or anything about fact-checking setting the agenda of debates. elementFails: yes. The image conveys information: it is an image of text naming the newsletter. Its text alternative does not serve the equivalent purpose (G94/G95), because it leaves out that text and the picture, and screen reader users hear the headline twice instead. The newsletter name does appear in the italic note below the byline, but that does not make the image decorative: it is not marked as such (null alt), and a non-null alt that names something else still fails. The claim, read in good faith, points at this defect: the alternative describes something the image does not show and leaves out what it does show. captureDiffers: no. The live HTML fetched on 2026-11-25 has the same img src and alt, with no figcaption, and the screenshot is a fully styled page.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the article's hero image (aside > figure). It is the generic cover of the newsletter (file digital-disfuncional-fundo-capa4x.png): the words "O Digital Disfuncional" over an abstract drawing of heads, eyes and crossed-out documents. Its alt is the article headline, which the h1 right below repeats word for word. claimTrue: yes, the alt names the article's subject (fact-checking in the electoral debates), which the picture does not show, and it leaves out everything the image does convey, including its text. elementFails: by G94 the alt does not carry the image's information (the newsletter name in the image), and if the image is treated as decorative it is not null either, so I lean yes. The skeptic's case against failing partly holds, though: the newsletter name appears as text in the first paragraph a little below ("publicado originalmente na newsletter O Digital Disfuncional"), so a screen reader user loses no information, and a headline alt on a featured image is a widespread convention that some auditors would call redundant (repeating the h1) rather than a 1.1.1 failure. Competent auditors would reasonably disagree on whether this fails, so the label is uncertain. If it does fail, the claim read in good faith names the failure. captureDiffers: no. The live HTML fetched on 2026-11-25 has the same img, src and alt, and the screenshot shows the styled page with the image as captured.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the Projor seal in the footer, the only content of a link to https://atlas.jor.br/vcp/18603, which opens in a new tab. It sits next to the 'Logo Ajor' and 'Selo IFCN' images, which are not links. The image reads 'Veiculo comprometido com o publico', '12', 'Projor'. claimTrue: no. The first half holds, since the image is all the link holds. The second half does not: the alt names the Projor seal, and the link leads to that seal's credential page. The vcp in the href is the seal's programme ('veiculo comprometido com o publico'). I opened the destination: it is the Atlas da Noticia card for Aos Fatos, showing its 'Selo Indicadores de Compromisso - 12/12' and the 12 transparency indicators of the 'Compromissos com o Publico' programme. That is the seal the image shows. elementFails: no. By G82/H30 and the rubric's R2 first test, the alternative read as the link's text names what the destination is about (the seal, the subject of the credential page). So the control has a name that describes its purpose, and 1.1.1 is met on this point. A longer alt that also gave the seal's printed wording or the Atlas da Noticia name, or a new-tab warning, would be better practice but is not required by 1.1.1. captureDiffers: no. The live HTML has the same link, href, target and alt, and the screenshot shows the seal as captured. Cause: Rampa did not read the destination, which settles that the alt names it.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the Projor seal in the footer ("Veículo comprometido com o público", 12, Projor), the only content of a link to https://atlas.jor.br/vcp/18603, with alt "Selo Projor". I opened the destination. It is the Atlas da Notícia card (Atlas da Notícia is Projor's project) for AOS FATOS under the Programa de Indicadores de Compromissos com o Público, which lists the 12 indicators: in other words, the verification page for that same seal. Read as the link's text, "Selo Projor" names the seal and its issuer, and the link opens that seal's certification card, so by the G82/H30 test the alternative does say what the link is for (R2: an alternative that names the page or thing the link opens describes its purpose). claimTrue: no. The first half holds (the image is all the link holds), but the alt does identify where the link goes. elementFails: no for 1.1.1. Some would want a longer alt such as "Selo Projor: veículo comprometido com o público", but that is a nicety, not a requirement. Rampa never read the destination ("not read by Rampa"), which is why it missed this, so the cause is context_missing. captureDiffers: no. The live HTML has the same link, href and alt (the target="_blank" has no bearing on 1.1.1), and the screenshot shows the badge in the styled footer, partly beside a support dialog that does not cover it.

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > form > div > div > input:nth-of-type(3)
subject: Search here...
message: The placeholder "Search here..." has a contrast of 2.80:1 with the field (#9f9999 on #ffffff). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input type="text" class="form-control" placeholder="Search here..." aria-label="Search here..." name="q" value="">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the Barristers' Register search field, whose only visible label is the placeholder "Search here..." (20px, weight 400, so not large text). claimTrue: the snapshot measured the placeholder colour #9f9999 from CSS on a #ffffff field; that pair computes to 2.80:1. elementFails: the live style sheet (core.min.css) sets .form-control::-webkit-input-placeholder and input::-webkit-input-placeholder to #9f9999 with no later override for .form-search, and the screenshot shows light grey placeholder text on a white pill field. Placeholder text is visible text that conveys information (here it is the field's only visible label), it is not an inactive component or decoration, so 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1 and 2.80:1 fails. captureDiffers: the live HTML and CSS fetched on 2026-11-25 match the capture (same input markup, same placeholder colour), and the screenshot is fully styled. The claim names the failure: true_positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the main register search field (input.form-control inside .form-search) with placeholder "Search here...". It has no visible label, so the placeholder is the only visible text that says what the field is for. The live stylesheet core.min.css sets the WebKit placeholder colour for .form-control and input to #9f9999. The .form-search .form-control rule gives a #fff background, and no more specific .form-search placeholder rule overrides either one; the #553c5c override only applies to .widget-search.mod-full-width. #9f9999 on #ffffff works out to about 2.80:1. The text is 20px at weight 400, which is not large text, so 4.5:1 is required. The screenshot crop shows light grey placeholder text on a white pill with the page fully styled. I looked for reasons to reject the finding. Understanding 1.4.3 says outright that the criterion "applies to text in the page, including placeholder text". The placeholder is neither inactive nor decorative, so the incidental exception does not apply. The live HTML and CSS match the capture, and no script changes the placeholder. No reason holds up, so this is a true positive.

ref: #news > div > div > div:nth-of-type(6) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > img

message: The text alternative "Microsoft outage" names a label, not what the image conveys here.

patch.ref: #news > div > div > div:nth-of-type(6) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > img

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is a news card image: a stock photo of network cables in a server, alt 'Microsoft outage'. It is not inside a link, and the card's h3 link 'Microsoft outage' follows it, with a summary. The claim is true of the capture: the alt is the story title, not a description of the cables. But the photo is a generic illustration that conveys nothing beyond the headline, and an alt naming the subject it illustrates serves its purpose here. 1.1.1 does not require describing a stock illustration's contents. At most the alt is redundant with the heading, and the better markup would be alt="" as decorative (an F38-style point). That is a different reason, and the claim, which asks for what the picture conveys, does not name it. The live page has the same card, image and alt. False positive.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the image of a news card, a generic stock photo of network cables plugged into a switch, with alt 'Microsoft outage'; it is not inside a link (the card's link is on its h3 'Microsoft outage', followed by the story summary). claimTrue: the alt repeats the card heading and does not describe the photo, so the sentence holds of the capture. elementFails: the photo carries no information of its own beyond illustrating the IT-outage story; an alt naming the story's topic serves that purpose (at worst it is redundant with the heading, where alt='' would be better practice), and it is not a filename or placeholder (F30). subject: hidden svg
message: This image is hidden from screen readers (aria-hidden="true"), but it conveys what the text around it does not say: "The slogan 'Building healthier lives'".

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the footer SVG uhb-c-footer__vision: a swirl mark with the words 'Building healthier lives', visible in the footer. It has aria-hidden="true", focusable=false, and no title or desc. Neither the snapshot nor the live HTML has the text 'healthier lives' anywhere else, so the trust's slogan or vision statement, shown as an image of text, is not available to assistive technology. It conveys text, so it is not pure decoration. It needs a text alternative, and hiding it fails 1.1.1. The claim states exactly this. The live footer markup is identical. True positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the footer SVG uhb-c-footer__vision: a logo mark and the slogan 'Building healthier lives' drawn as paths, with aria-hidden='true', no title or text, and no visible or hidden text anywhere on the page with those words (the snapshot and the live HTML have no 'healthier'). claimTrue: yes, it is hidden and the surrounding footer text (social links, Privacy, Terms, copyright) does not say it. ref: html > body > header > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > a > span:nth-of-type(2)
subject: NHS Foundation Trust
message: The text "NHS Foundation Trust" has at most 3.18:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ffffff on #5795d0), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a pseudo-element). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The element is the descriptor 'NHS Foundation Trust' (15px, bold) inside the header logo link, under the NHS lozenge and 'University Hospitals Birmingham'. The claim is true of the capture: white on #5795d0 from the pseudo-element is 3.17:1. Capture: the header is transparent and its ::before lays rgba(0,94,184,0.66) over a fixed full-page photo (.uhb-c-bg-image, page-background-home-2.jpg, a greyscale ward scene) that 'shows through the header'. In Rampa's full-page capture that photo sat at the bottom of the page, not behind the header, so the header read as flat #5795d0 (the screenshot shows #c6dbef, the same colour under the cookie notice's 66% white wash). A live render in Edge at 1280x800 shows the photo behind the header, and its pixels match a model of the photo under the blue overlay. So on the page users receive, the background behind the text is not a flat #5795d0. The cookie notice washes the whole page until it is dismissed; I judged the header after dismissal, since text behind a modal wash is not what is assessed. Live at scroll 0, the letters 'NH' sit on a light part of the photo at about 3.2:1, and the rest of the text is at 5.3:1 or more. This is normal-size text, so 4.5:1 applies, and the 'NH' falls short of it. But the text is the trust's organisational logo (NHS lozenge plus organisation name and descriptor, the link classed uhb-c-header__logo), and the 1.4.3 logotype exception ('text that is part of a logo or brand name') arguably exempts it. My lean is that the exception applies (no failure). Competent auditors would reasonably disagree: some treat live HTML header text as subject to 4.5:1. Hence uncertain.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the 'NHS Foundation Trust' descriptor (15px bold, white) inside the header logo link href='/' whose content is the NHS lozenge SVG, 'University Hospitals Birmingham' and this descriptor (markup commented 'NHS Logo', classes uhb-c-header__logo-organisation-descriptor): the NHS organisational logo lockup set in HTML text. claimTrue: in the capture it is #ffffff on a flat #5795d0 behind a ::before, 3.18:1, so the sentence holds of the capture. elementFails: 1.4.3's Logotypes exception says 'Text that is part of a logo or brand name has no contrast requirement'; this line is part of the trust's logo and of its brand name 'University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust', so no ratio is required. Without the exception it would be normal-size text needing 4.5:1, and on the real page the first letters sit on light parts of the photo at about 3.2-3.6:1 at 1280x800 and 1366x768 (but pass at 1536x864 and 1920x1080), so the exemption is what decides it. captureDiffers: the header is transparent with a ::before of rgba(0,94,184,0.66), and the page has a fixed, full-viewport background photo (.uhb-c-bg-image, page-background-home-2.jpg, z-index -1) that the site's CSS says 'shows through the header'. Rampa's full-page capture painted that fixed photo at the bottom of the page (it is visible behind the CQC box at y~3580-3925), so behind the header it had white and measured a flat #5795d0 (66% NHS blue over white). A headless Edge render of the live page at 1280x800 shows the blue-tinted photo behind the header; recomputing from the photo, the background under the nav text ranges from about 3.2:1 to 10:1 against white, never below 3.18:1 (3.18:1 is the case where the photo is pure white). Label false_positive: the rule applied a contrast requirement to logotype text that 1.4.3 exempts.

subject: logo
message: The text alternative "logo" is a file name or a placeholder.

patch.ref: #CybotCookiebotDialogPoweredbyImage

auditor.label: true_positive

ref: #id_first_name
message: The field "First name" asks for the user's first name but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="given-name" is missing. Chromium's own form check flags this field too.

patch.ref: #id_first_name
patch.before: <input type="text" name="first_name" placeholder="First name" required="" id="id_first_name">
patch.after: <input type="text" name="first_name" placeholder="First name" required="" id="id_first_name" autocomplete="given-name">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the "First name" input of the newsletter sign-up form ("Sign up to get CKD support and information by email"), which collects the visitor's own details. claimTrue: the captured input has no autocomplete attribute, so autocomplete="given-name" is indeed missing, and the snapshot records Chromium's FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError issue on this field. elementFails: 1.3.5 requires the purpose of an input collecting information about the user to be programmatically determinable when the purpose is one of the listed input purposes (here given-name); with no autocomplete token (H98) nothing exposes that purpose, and the live HTML and the rendered snapshot both lack it, so the field fails. captureDiffers: the live page's HTML, fetched today, has the same input with no autocomplete attribute; no difference. True positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The newsletter sign-up field "First name" (input#id_first_name, name="first_name", type="text") asks for the visitor's own first name so they can join the mailing list ("Yes, please add me to the mailing list"). claimTrue: the captured input has no autocomplete attribute, and the snapshot records Chromium's form issue FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError for it, so the remark about Chromium's check is also true. elementFails: given-name is an input purpose listed in WCAG 2.1 section 7, and the field collects information about the user. Without autocomplete (H98) or another mechanism, its purpose cannot be programmatically determined, so it fails 1.3.5. I looked for a way out: no hidden or third-party use of the field applies; it is plainly the user's own name. Chromium also infers the purpose from the name attribute, but that is a heuristic and not programmatic determination. captureDiffers: the live HTML has the identical input, with no autocomplete. True positive.

subject: First name
message: The placeholder "First name" has a contrast of 2.54:1 with the field (#9ca3af on #ffffff). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input type="text" name="first_name" placeholder="First name" required="" id="id_first_name">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the sign-up form's "First name" text input; it has a visible <label for> "First name" above it and a placeholder that repeats it. claimTrue: the snapshot measured the placeholder at #9ca3af on #ffffff, 20px, weight 400, and I recompute 2.54:1 from those colours. elementFails: the live stylesheet (main_kcuk.min.493deb9fc9c3.css) sets input::placeholder{color:#9ca3af;opacity:1} and the field is white, so users see the placeholder at 2.54:1, below the 4.5:1 that 1.4.3 requires for text of this size; placeholder text is visible text and falls under none of 1.4.3's exceptions (it is not inactive, decorative, invisible, part of a picture or a logotype), and repeating the visible label does not exempt it. captureDiffers: the live HTML has the same input and placeholder and the live CSS gives the same colour; in the full-page screenshot the fixed Cookiebot dialog is stamped over the form, but that is a screenshot artefact that does not touch the colours. The claim names the failure: true positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The newsletter sign-up field "First name" (input#id_first_name) has a visible <label> above it, and its placeholder "First name" repeats that label. claimTrue: the snapshot records the placeholder colour #9ca3af taken from CSS on a #ffffff field, 20px weight 400, 2.54:1, as stated. elementFails: the live stylesheet main_kcuk.min.493deb9fc9c3.css sets input::placeholder{color:#9ca3af;opacity:1} with no override for the sign-up form, and the visible part of the field in the screenshot is white, so users get 2.54:1, below 4.5:1 (20px regular is not large text, and it would also miss 3:1). I looked for a way out: the visible label makes the placeholder redundant, but redundancy is not one of 1.4.3's exceptions (inactive component, pure decoration, invisible, part of a picture, logotype), and Understanding 1.4.3 says the criterion "applies to text in the page, including placeholder text". captureDiffers: the live HTML has the same input and the live CSS has the same placeholder colour. The cookie dialog that covers the form in the stitched full-page screenshot is a screenshot artefact and does not affect this text. True positive.

patch.from: Boy, 12, charged after investigation into Epsom 'violent disorder' that followed mistaken rape report
patch.to: Police officers in riot gear standing in front of a police van.

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The image is a news-teaser thumbnail that is not inside a link (live markup: div.Teaser_cover-wrapper > img, then a separate h3 headline link whose aria-label is the same headline); its alt repeats the headline word for word. The crop shows police officers in riot gear with shields beside police vans; the alt says a 12-year-old boy was charged after an investigation into the disorder, which the photo does not show, so the claim holds of the capture. The live page has the same teaser, src and alt. Whether this fails 1.1.1 is a point competent auditors split on: read by G94 the photo is informative and the headline does not present what it shows, and if it is taken as eye-candy it should have a null alt (F38's test); but many auditors treat a headline alt on a teaser photo as an alternative that identifies the story, merely redundant with the adjacent link (a best-practice issue, as in axe's image-redundant-alt). My lean is a failure, but reasonable disagreement makes the label uncertain.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: Teaser thumbnail in the top group; the crop shows police officers in riot gear with shields beside marked police vans (file 0_Epsom-sexual-assault.jpg). The img sits in the teaser's cover div, outside any link; the h3 headline link with the same text follows it in the same article. So the alt repeats the adjacent headline and does not describe the photo. claimTrue: the alt reports a 12-year-old being charged after an investigation, which the picture does not show. elementFails: the alt names the event the photo depicts ('Epsom violent disorder'), but not what the picture shows (the riot police response). A strict G94 reading fails it for the claim's reason. The teaser reading (an illustration of the adjacent headline, ideally alt='') passes it, or faults only redundancy, which the claim does not name. Competent auditors would disagree. The live page could not be compared: curl got an AWS WAF challenge (HTTP 202, empty) and WebFetch was redirected to tollbit.getsurrey.co.uk, a version for automated clients that is not what people receive. The capture itself shows no sign of differing (full styling, real photos, the consent dialog, a 10,319 px page).

skeptic.rationale: [visual context] The element is the comment-count link (aria-label '"Comments"', visible '1 Comments') under the 'Mercedes exploded near Heathrow' card of the Mantis 'Similar articles to this' carousel, pointing to that article's #comments-wrapper. auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the magnifying-glass svg (no role, no title, no aria-label) inside the Blogger search widget's label.search-submit-container, beside a display:none <input type=submit>. The claim is not true of the capture: the text next to it does say what the icon means, since the search field's aria-label and its visible placeholder are both 'Pesquisar este blog' (search this blog), and the widget sits in a role=search region under a heading with the same text. Also, the captured AX tree exposes the svg as an unnamed image that is not ignored, so 'hidden from screen readers' does not strictly hold either. For 1.1.1 the icon is redundant with that text: it identifies the search field that is already named, and the form submits with Enter from the field. It adds no information that a text alternative would need to carry. An unnamed svg with no explicit role is not in scope of the ACT image-name rules, and screen readers generally skip it. Adding aria-hidden='true' would be better practice, but that is not the failure the claim describes, which says the icon carries unique information. Whether the hidden submit input is keyboard-operable is a separate matter, not 1.1.1 on this svg. The live HTML I fetched has identical markup (same label, svg and hidden submit input), and the screenshot is the fully styled page, so the capture does not differ. skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the magnifying-glass svg (sprite ic_search_black_24dp, no role, no title, no aria-hidden) inside the Blogger search widget's label, next to a textbox named "Pesquisar este blog" by aria-label and placeholder, all within a role=search landmark under a heading "Pesquisar este blog". claimTrue: no. A live fetch on 2026-11-25 returned the same widget markup (aria-label, placeholder, hidden submit, unnamed svg) and the same CSS, and the screenshot is fully styled. ref: #map_6b0669b637dda > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(4) > div > a:nth-of-type(1)
subject: Leaflet
message: The text "Leaflet" has at most 4.15:1 contrast with what is behind it (#7bbccd on #d9cfbd…#f8fef8), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (an image in the element). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <a href="https://leafletjs.com" title="A JavaScript library for interactive maps">

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The element is the "Leaflet" link in the map attribution, 11px text in #0078a8 (live CSS) on the attribution's translucent white over the map. Most of the word sits on #effef0, where it reaches about 4.73:1 and passes; its last letters sit over a darker park area (#e7f1e2, about 4.25:1) and a brown map icon (about 3:1), so a per-letter G18 test fails there. The claim's "at most 4.15:1" uses anti-aliased pixels (#7bbccd) and is not true as worded, since the best contrast is above 4.5:1. Whether text that mostly passes but has a letter over a darker map detail fails 1.4.3 is a point competent auditors would disagree on, so uncertain.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The "Leaflet" attribution link (11px, weight 400, title "A JavaScript library for interactive maps") over the map. The rule took its foreground from anti-aliased pixels (#7bbccd, foregroundFrom "pixels"); Understanding 1.4.3 says to use the specified colours, not the text as rendered. With the real link colour #0078A8 on the attribution's rgba(255,255,255,0.7) over the tiles (live, unchanged), the background under most of the word is #effef0, which gives 4.73:1 and passes. So "at most 4.15:1" is false (claimTrue no), and the claim's worst case comes from the flag icon and map features. However, the last letter or so sits on a #e7f1e2 patch (4.25:1), with a few map-feature pixels lower. With the text mostly passing and a sliver below 4.5:1 on a varied map background (the ACT rule says there is "no clear method" when some pixels pass and others do not), whether the link fails cannot be settled, and auditors would disagree.

The claim's "at most 3.59:1" comes from anti-aliased pixels (#50a2bc), not the real text colour, so the sentence is not true as worded, but it points at the real defect: the link text is under 4.5:1 against what is behind it. Fails 1.4.3; the attribution is a link, not incidental text.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The "OpenStreetMap" link in the Leaflet attribution (11px, weight 400) over the map. Skeptic check: the snapshot shows the rule took the foreground from rendered pixels (#50a2bc), an anti-aliased tint. Understanding 1.4.3 says to use the colours from the user agent or stylesheets "rather than the text as presented on screen", so the stated 3.59:1 and #50a2bc are wrong, and claimTrue is no. ref: html > body > a:nth-of-type(2)
subject: Falar no WhatsApp — (21) 99571-1987
message: The icon of this link ("Falar no WhatsApp — (21) 99571-1987") has at most 1.98:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ffffff on #25d366). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).
html: <a class="m2br-wa-float" href="https://wa.me/5521995711987?text=Ol%C3%A1%2C%20vim%20pelo%20site%20do%20Teatro%20Riachuelo" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" aria-label="Falar no WhatsApp — (21) 99571-1987" role="link">

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The element is the fixed floating WhatsApp link (aria-label "Falar no WhatsApp — (21) 99571-1987"): a 56px #25D366 circle holding only the white WhatsApp glyph (fill currentColor, color #fff). The snapshot and the live CSS both give #ffffff on #25d366, which is 1.98:1, and the glyph is all the control shows, so the sentence is true of the capture. Whether that fails 1.4.11 is debatable: the glyph is the WhatsApp brand logo in WhatsApp's own brand colours, and Understanding 1.4.11 says logos are exempt as essential and that the exemption "carries over" to a user interface component that is a logo, while other auditors treat such a glyph as an icon under G207 and fail it. I lean to a pass under the logo exemption, but competent auditors would disagree, so uncertain. In the screenshot the button sits under the cookie banner, which does not change its colours; the live page has the same CSS.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The floating link (a.m2br-wa-float, aria-label "Falar no WhatsApp — (21) 99571-1987") is a 56px circle with background #25D366 holding only the white WhatsApp glyph (the standard WhatsApp path); live CSS matches the capture (color #fff, background #25D366), so white on #25D366 is 1.98:1 and the glyph is all the control shows: the claim is true of the capture. Skeptic reason: this is the WhatsApp brand logo in the brand's own colours. Understanding 1.4.11 says brand logos "presented in the brand's specific colors" fall under the essential exception and that "normatively the exemption 'carries over' to the user interface component"; authors are "encouraged (but not required)" to add a contrasting aspect. The author-choice clause does not apply, because this is how the logo is normally presented. By that reading the link meets 1.4.11. Auditors who apply G207 to any icon-only control, or who treat the green circle as the author's button background and not part of the logo, would fail it, so competent auditors would reasonably disagree. In the capture and live, the float sits under the cookie banner until cookies are accepted; after that it shows with the same colours, so the capture does not differ in a way that matters.

ref: #rd-text_field-mf2n6xpu
subject: textbox
message: The browser exposes this element as a textbox but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "textbox", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).
html: <input id="rd-text_field-mf2n6xpu" class="bricks-form__input required js-text js-field-name" name="name" type="text" data-use-type="STRING" placeholder="Nome *" required="required">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the name input of the footer newsletter form. Its <label for> ("Nome*") is display:none, and Chromium computes an empty accessible name: the snapshot records the browser name "", and on the live page, in a Chromium browser (Edge), the CDP name sources show the hidden label giving "" and the placeholder "Nome *" marked superseded, so the field is exposed as an unnamed textbox. Its name is therefore not programmatically determinable in Chromium browsers, which fails 4.1.2, and the claim states that.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: Newsletter "Nome" input: its <label for> "Nome*" is display:none, and the only visible label is the placeholder "Nome *". The capture's CDP name is "", so the claim is true of the capture. Live in a real Chromium browser (Edge), the computed name is again "": Chromium takes the hidden label as the name source, giving an empty string, and marks the placeholder "superseded". So in Chromium the field has no accessible name, which fails 4.1.2. Skeptic reason that partly holds: HTML-AAM says that if the name "is still empty" after the label and title steps, the placeholder is used, which would give "Nome *". ACT rule e086e5 (Passed Example 5) accepts a placeholder as the name, axe-core passes a non-empty placeholder, and screen readers often announce a placeholder exposed as a hint. Whether the field fails therefore depends on whether one judges Chromium's exposed name or the spec's computation, and competent auditors would reasonably disagree. (The hidden label also bears on 3.3.2, but that is not this finding.)

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: 'Servidores' is an unselected quicktabs tab link in the Notícias (Gerais / Servidores / Estudantes) block. subject: Boletins de Serviço
message: The text "Boletins de Serviço" has at most 3.86:1 contrast with what is behind it (#777777 on #eeeeee), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (an element over or under it). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: 'Boletins de Serviço' is an unselected quicktabs tab link in the Documentos (Editais / Boletins de Serviço / Portarias) block. The screenshot pixels at its bounds are #777777 text on #eeeeee (3.86:1), and the live style sheet sets exactly that (ul.quicktabs-tabs li a: color #777; background #eee) for unselected tabs; the text is about 16px at weight 600, not large text, so 4.5:1 applies, and an unselected tab is an operable control, not an inactive component. The page offers an 'Alto contraste' switch (G174), and its high-contrast style sheet turns these tabs white on #2a2a2a, but the switch itself is #fff on #009045 at 11.2px (4.14:1), so it does not meet G174's own test and does not rescue the default presentation. The live page has the same markup and CSS; the splash overlay over the top of the capture does not reach this tab, so nothing in the capture changes the claim. True positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The unselected 'Boletins de Serviço' tab of the Documentos quicktabs. Live CSS #777 on #eee; screenshot pixels at its bounds #777777 on #eeeeee, 3.86:1 at 16px weight 600, so it needs 4.5:1 and fails. It is an operable tab; the 'Alto contraste' switcher does not satisfy G174 (switcher link 4.14:1, first click is a no-op because of an id mismatch, alternate view still has failing text). Live page matches the capture.

ref: #edit-search-api-views-fulltext
subject: Pesquisar
message: The placeholder "Pesquisar" has a contrast of 2.92:1 with the field (#888888 on #e9e9e9). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input type="text" id="edit-search-api-views-fulltext" name="search_api_views_fulltext" value="" size="30" maxlength="128" class="form-text required error" placeholder="Pesquisar" minlength="3" required="required">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The header search field gets placeholder="Pesquisar" from the site's own script (attr('placeholder','Pesquisar') on search_api_views_fulltext), and the live CSS sets ::-webkit-input-placeholder color #888 on #edit-search-api-views-fulltext background #e9e9e9 !important: 2.92:1 at 13px, below 4.5:1. The placeholder is visible text and, with the label hidden, the only on-screen text saying what the field is for, so 1.4.3 applies. The 'Alto contraste' switch is itself 4.14:1, so G174 does not apply. The screenshot cannot show the field (the splash overlay covers the header), but the live HTML, script and CSS give the same colours as the capture. True positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The header search field; the site script adds placeholder='Pesquisar', and the live CSS sets '::-webkit-input-placeholder{color:#888}' and '#edit-search-api-views-fulltext{background-color:#e9e9e9 !important}', giving 2.92:1 in Chrome at 13px. Understanding 1.4.3 states the criterion applies to placeholder text, and here the placeholder is the only visible label (the real label '«nenhum»' is display:none). The field is operable, so no inactive-component exception. The high-contrast sheet does not restyle the field or placeholder, and the switcher fails G174 anyway. The screenshot's top is covered by a splash overlay, but the CSS and served HTML are the same live as in the capture.

ref: html
subject: Unipampa | Universidade Federal do Pampa
message: The page title "Unipampa | Universidade Federal do Pampa" says nothing about this page.

patch.ref: html
patch.before: <title>Unipampa | Universidade Federal do Pampa</title>
patch.after: <title>Portal Institucional | Unipampa</title>

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the university portal's home page (https://unipampa.edu.br/portal/), and its title 'Unipampa | Universidade Federal do Pampa' names the institution the whole page is about; for a home page the site or organisation name describes its topic and purpose (G88), so the claim that the title says nothing about the page is false and 2.4.2 is met. The live page has the same title. The model had the title, URL and content and judged wrongly: false positive, model_error.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The title 'Unipampa | Universidade Federal do Pampa' is on the university portal's home page (https://unipampa.edu.br/portal/), whose h1 is the Unipampa logo. For a home page the site and organisation name is exactly its topic and purpose, so the title identifies the page and 2.4.2 is met (F25 is not triggered). The claim that it 'says nothing about this page' is false. The model had the URL and the title and judged wrongly. The live title is the same.

ref: #block-locale-language > div > div > ul > li:nth-of-type(2) > a
subject: English
message: "English" is in English, but it inherits the page's language (pt-br): a screen reader mispronounces the language's name. Add lang="en" to the link.

patch.ref: #block-locale-language > div > div > ul > li:nth-of-type(2) > a
patch.before: <a href="/portal/en" class="language-link" xml:lang="en">
patch.after: <a href="/portal/en" class="language-link" xml:lang="en" lang="en">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The language switcher link 'English' carries only xml:lang="en" and no lang attribute; the page is served as text/html, where xml:lang has no effect on language processing, so the link inherits html lang="pt-br". Understanding 3.1.2 gives this exact case as an example ('Alternative language links': the name of each language in that language, identified with a lang attribute, H58), and a language name is not one of the exceptions. The live HTML is unchanged (same xml:lang-only markup); the splash overlay hiding the header in the screenshot does not touch a markup claim. True positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The 'English' link of the language switcher in a page with lang='pt-br'. It carries only xml:lang='en'; the page is served as text/html (checked the response header), where the HTML spec says an xml:lang attribute in no namespace has no effect on language processing, and Blink and Gecko only read xml:lang in the XML namespace, so the link inherits pt-br. Understanding 3.1.2 says single words count unless it is not clear a change of language was intended; here the change is plainly intended (the author even wrote xml:lang), 'English' is not the Portuguese word (inglês) and is not a proper name used across languages untranslated. The live HTML is identical to the capture.

ref: #block-locale-language > div > div > ul > li:nth-of-type(3) > a
subject: Español

patch.before: <a href="/portal/es" class="language-link" xml:lang="es">
patch.after: <a href="/portal/es" class="language-link" xml:lang="es" lang="es">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The language switcher link 'Español' carries only xml:lang="es" and no lang attribute; the page is served as text/html, where xml:lang has no effect on language processing, so the link inherits html lang="pt-br". Understanding 3.1.2 gives this exact case as an example ('Alternative language links': the name of each language in that language, identified with a lang attribute, H58), and a language name is not one of the exceptions. The live HTML is unchanged (same xml:lang-only markup); the splash overlay hiding the header in the screenshot does not touch a markup claim. True positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The 'Español' link of the language switcher, marked only with xml:lang='es' in a text/html document with lang='pt-br'; in text/html that attribute has no effect, so the link's language is pt-br. Its Portuguese spelling is 'Espanhol', so a pt-BR voice may pronounce it close, but Understanding 3.1.2 applies the pronunciation test only when it is in doubt whether a change of language was intended, and in a language switcher (with the author's own xml:lang) the change is clearly intended. Not a proper name, technical term or vernacular word. Live HTML matches the capture.

ref: #edit-search-api-views-fulltext
subject: textbox
message: The browser exposes this element as a textbox but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "textbox", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).
html: <input type="text" id="edit-search-api-views-fulltext" name="search_api_views_fulltext" value="" size="30" maxlength="128" class="form-text required error" placeholder="Pesquisar" minlength="3" required="required">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The search textbox's only label is <label for> with the text '«nenhum»' (Drupal's empty-label placeholder), hidden by .views-exposed-form label{display:none}. The browser's accessibility tree in the capture records the label relation and a computed name of "" (it did not fall back to the script-added placeholder), so the control has no programmatically determined name in Chrome (F68, ACT 'form field has non-empty accessible name'); and in a browser that did use the hidden label, the name '«nenhum»' ('none') would still not identify the field. The live HTML has the same hidden '«nenhum»' label and the same script, so the capture matches what users receive. True positive.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The header search textbox. Its associated label holds the junk text '«nenhum»' ('none') and is display:none (.views-exposed-form label), and a script adds placeholder='Pesquisar'. Chrome's tree in the capture gives the name '' with a labelledby relation to that hidden label: the empty label wins and the placeholder is not used, so in Chrome the field has no accessible name (ACT e086e5 fails), which is what the claim says. But a concrete counter-reading holds up: HTML-AAM falls through to the placeholder when the label yields no usable text, ACT e086e5 Passed Example 5 accepts a placeholder as the name, axe-core's label rule passes a non-empty placeholder, accname 1.2 would even take the hidden label's '«nenhum»', and Chrome still exposes the placeholder, which major screen readers announce, so 'announces only textbox' is overstated. Whether this fails 4.1.2 or only 3.3.2/2.4.6 is something competent auditors would split on. The live HTML, CSS and script match the capture.

message: The text "Última atualização: novembro/2026" has at most 4.12:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ffffff80 on #004689…#003574), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a background image). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

ref: #select2-select1-container
subject: textbox
message: The browser exposes this element as a textbox but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "textbox", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).
html: <span id="select2-select1-container" class="select2-selection__rendered filtro" title="Escolha o estado" role="textbox">

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The element is the Select2 rendered span for the state filter (role=textbox, read-only, title="Escolha o estado", text "Escolha o estado"), inside the focusable combobox. claimTrue: the CDP node has role textbox and name "" with value "Escolha o estado", so the claim about the browser's computation holds, though its gloss overstates since the value is exposed. elementFails: the span cannot be focused or operated; the control users tab to is the parent combobox, named "Escolha o estado" through aria-labelledby and exposing role, value and collapsed state, and the title would name the span by the accessible name computation in other engines. Chromium still exposes an unnamed textbox widget, ARIA requires a name for that role, and Select2 later dropped the role as a defect. Competent auditors would disagree on whether the inner span is a separate user interface component failing 4.1.2, so uncertain. The widget's stronger problem lies elsewhere: the sr-only <label for=select1> "Localidade" names only the aria-hidden native select, so the combobox's name is its placeholder and then the chosen state. captureDiffers: the live HTML has the same select1 markup and the same Select2 4.0.6-rc.0; no difference found.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is Select2 4.0.6-rc.0's rendered-selection span for the state (Localidade) filter: role=textbox, read-only, not focusable on its own, with title="Escolha o estado" and text "Escolha o estado", nested in the Select2 span with role=combobox (aria-labelledby pointing at this span). claimTrue: yes, the captured CDP tree from Edge 158 gives this textbox the name "" with no name source and no description, so the sentence holds of the capture. elementFails: cannot_tell. Reasons against a failure hold up: the author supplied a title, which accname step 2I makes the accessible name and which axe-core's aria-input-field-name accepts (non-empty-title), so the name is author-supplied data that user agents can extract, and Chromium not exposing it looks like a browser quirk rather than missing content. Also, by WCAG's definition a user interface component is what users perceive as one control: this span is the display inside the combobox, which has a role and a name. Against that, the Chromium tree users of Chrome or Edge get does expose a nameless textbox, and ARIA requires a name for that role. The real defects here are elsewhere: the span's textbox role misrepresents a non-editable display, and the combobox's name is the placeholder or selected value while the native select's sr-only label is hidden with it. captureDiffers: no, the live HTML loads the same Select2 4.0.6-rc.0 on the same selects, and the screenshot shows the same filter. Competent auditors would disagree on whether this span fails 4.1.2 for a missing name, so the label is uncertain.

ref: #block-views-block-cards-capa-portal-block-3 > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > span > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > img
subject: Revista Mais POA
message: The text alternative "Revista Mais POA" describes something the image does not show.

patch.ref: #block-views-block-cards-capa-portal-block-3 > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > span > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > img

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the card image of the 'Revista Mais POA' card in the 'Mais Proteção' block, alt="Revista Mais POA"; it is not inside a link (the card's overlay link is a sibling) and its alt repeats the card's h3 'Revista Mais POA'. The image (crop and screenshot) is a banner whose only text is 'PORTO ALEGRE MAIS PROTEGIDA' over a photo of flood-protection earthworks; it shows no magazine name or magazine, so the claim is true of the capture. The destination page confirms 'Porto Alegre mais protegida' is the title of the 8th edition, and that title appears nowhere else in the card (the description only paraphrases the theme). The alternative therefore does not present the same information as the image (G94 test; W3C's images-of-text guidance asks the alternative to contain the image's words), so the image fails 1.1.1, and the claim, read in good faith, points at that: the alt names something not shown and leaves out what the image conveys. The live HTML has the same img, src and alt as the snapshot and the screenshot matches, so the capture does not differ.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the card image of the 'Revista Mais POA' card in the 'Mais Proteção' section, alt 'Revista Mais POA'. The first half of the claim holds. message: The icon of this link ("Bluesky") has at most 2.56:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ffffff on #00aaff). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The Bluesky share link shows only a white butterfly glyph on a circle that the theme paints #0af (.brxe-post-sharing.brand-colors .bluesky), as in the screenshot. White on #0af is 2.56:1, so the claim holds. This blue is the Bricks theme's choice, not Bluesky's brand blue (about #1185fe, from general knowledge; I did not check a brand source). White on the brand blue gives 3.6:1. Understanding 1.4.11 says a logo given a low-contrast presentation by the author's choice is not exempt, so the logo exemption does not cover this icon. The icon is the only visual information that identifies the control, and the circle is 2.46:1 against the page. The link fails 3:1 as claimed. The live HTML and CSS match the capture.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The Bluesky share link shows only a white butterfly on a #00aaff circle (theme rule .brand-colors .bluesky{background-color:#0af}); pixels give #ffffff on #00aaff = 2.56:1 and the circle is 2.46:1 against the page, with no visible text. Skeptic check on the logo exemption: Bluesky's brand blue is #1185FE/#0085FF, on which a white butterfly reaches 3.6:1, so the lighter #00aaff is the theme's choice, not the brand's, and Understanding 1.4.11 says such an author-chosen low-contrast presentation of a logo is not 'essential' and not exempt. The live page (fetched 2026-11-25) has the same markup (ul.brxe-post-sharing.brand-colors, aria-label only, title on the li) and the theme CSS frontend-layer.min.css still sets color:#fff on the list and the same brand background colours; the screenshot is fully styled, so the capture matches what users receive. The claim names the failure.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the round 96px thumbnail in the first '+Colunas' card on the home page, inside a link whose text is the kicker 'Levantamento' and the headline about elderly people abandoned in hospitals. The crop and the screenshot show a head-and-shoulders portrait of a man; the destination article uses the same image file with alt="Ronaldo Rocha" next to 'COLUNA Ronaldo Rocha', so it is the columnist's portrait. Its alt on the home page, 'Idosos estão abandonados em hospitais de São Luís', is the story's topic: it describes nothing the picture shows, and the card names the columnist nowhere in text. The alternative does not serve the image's purpose (identifying the columnist), and if the image were taken as redundant it should be null (F39); either way it fails 1.1.1, which is what the claim says. The live HTML fetched today has the same img and alt, so the capture matches what users receive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The img is the round 96px thumbnail of a '+Colunas' card, inside a link that also holds the kicker h3 'Levantamento', the headline h2 and the time. The crop and the screenshot show a head-and-shoulders portrait of a man; its alt 'Idosos estão abandonados em hospitais de São Luís' is the caption of the article's lead photo (the destination page shows that caption under its figure and gives this same image file the alt 'Ronaldo Rocha', the columnist). So the claim is true of the capture. I looked for a way it could pass: the link has its own text, so the image does not need to name the link (H30 applies only to image-only links), and H2 would want a null alt or one that supplements it by describing the picture. This alt does neither. If the portrait conveys who wrote the column, the alt leaves that out, and the columnist's name is not in the card's text. If the portrait is decorative, a non-null alt fails F38. Either way the text alternative is not equivalent, and the claim names exactly that. The live HTML fetched now has the same src and alt, so the capture does not differ.

ref: #switch-button
subject: checkbox
message: The browser exposes this element as a checkbox but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "checkbox", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the 'Modo Noturno' dark-mode switch in the off-canvas menu (#mp-menu-v2): <input id="switch-button" type="checkbox"> inside <label for="switch-button" class="switch"> that holds only the input and an empty slider span. The text 'Modo Noturno 🌙' is in a sibling div, not in the label and not referenced by aria-labelledby, so the snapshot's accessibility tree gives the checkbox an empty name while exposing it as a focusable checkbox. A screen reader announces only 'checkbox, not checked' when the menu is open, so it fails 4.1.2 (name), as the claim says. The live HTML has the same markup.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The input#switch-button is the night-mode toggle in the off-canvas menu (nav#mp-menu-v2). In the live HTML it sits inside <label for="switch-button" class="switch">, but that label contains only <span class="slider round">. In the live stylesheet, .slider:before has content "" and .switch input is 0x0 with opacity 0, so the label provides no text. The visible 'Modo Noturno 🌙' is in a sibling div with no programmatic association (no aria-labelledby). The snapshot's browser AX data shows a checkbox labelled by that empty label and no name, so the claim holds. I found nothing that gives it a name on the page users receive: no aria-label, title or generated text. A screen reader would announce only 'checkbox, not checked' when the menu is opened, which fails 4.1.2's name requirement (it also falls short of 1.3.1/3.3.2 label practice). The live page matches the capture.

auditor.rationale: The element is the small icon (src icon-store.svg) inside the top-bar link "Seja um franqueado" (to /seja-franqueado). The crop shows a storefront/awning icon, not a login icon, so alt="Icon Login" describes something the image does not show, and the claim holds. The icon repeats the adjacent link text and should be ignored by assistive technology (alt=""). Instead it has a non-null, wrong alternative, which F39 names as a failure. The skeptic's best counter is that the link text already gives the purpose, so the icon is decorative. That does not save it: 1.1.1 then requires the icon to be ignorable by assistive technology, and a non-null alt on such an image is F39. If the icon is read as meaningful instead, "Icon Login" is a wrong alternative that tells users about a login that is not there. Either way the element fails 1.1.1. auditor.rationale: The element is the small icon (src icon-locate.svg) inside the top-bar link "Nossas lojas" (to /nossas-lojas). The crop shows a location pin, not a login icon, so alt="Icon Login" describes something the image does not show, and the claim holds. The icon is redundant with the link text and should have a null alternative. Its non-null, false alternative fails 1.1.1 (F39), and it puts "Icon Login" into the link's name ("Icon Login Nossas lojas"), misleading screen-reader users about the link. The live HTML has the identical markup, so the capture does not differ. The claim names the real defect.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is a 20x21 icon inside the "Nossas lojas" link (href /nossas-lojas). Its file is icon-locate.svg, and both the SVG path and the crop show a map location pin, not a login icon. alt="Icon Login", copied from another icon, is announced: the browser names the link "Icon Login Nossas lojas". The visible link text gives the purpose, so the icon is redundant. A redundant icon should have a null alt (F39); if it is read as meaningful, the alternative is wrong. Either way it fails 1.1.1, and no technique makes it pass. The claim names the mismatch between the alt and the picture. The live HTML has the same img and alt, so the capture does not differ.

subject: Logo
message: The text alternative "Logo" is a file name or a placeholder.

patch.ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > a > span > img

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header logo, an img with alt="Logo" that is the only content of the link to "/" (the link's accessible name is "Logo"). The crop shows the orange ARTWALK wordmark. "Logo" is a generic placeholder word, so the claim holds of the capture. As the only content of a link the image is a control, and 1.1.1 requires a name that describes its purpose (H30); "Logo" names neither the brand nor the home destination and does not convey the image-of-text "ARTWALK" (F30: placeholder text as an alternative). The live HTML fetched with curl still has alt="Logo" on the same image in the same link, so nothing in the capture differs for this claim. The claim names the real defect.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the header logo, an SVG wordmark reading ARTWALK, and it is the only content of the home link (href "/", no aria-label or title; the browser names the link "Logo"). alt="Logo" is not a file name, but it is generic placeholder text of the kind F30 lists ("image", "picture"): it names the type of image, not the brand text it shows or where the link goes. That fails 1.1.1 under F30 and H30 (an image that is the only content of a link must describe its function, e.g. "Artwalk" or "Artwalk, página inicial"). I looked for something that would cure it and found nothing: no visible text, no aria-label, no title. The page title is not the control's name. The live HTML fetched today has the same markup and alt="Logo" (only the class is lazyload, before the script runs). The full-page screenshot's header band is blank, but the crop shows the wordmark, so no capture difference touches the claim. The claim's "placeholder" names the real defect.

ref: #downshift-0-input
subject: Encontre na Artwalk
message: The placeholder "Encontre na Artwalk" has a contrast of 2.77:1 with the field (#8c8f94 on #eceded). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input class="vtex-styleguide-9-x-input ma0 border-box vtex-styleguide-9-x-hideDecorators vtex-styleguide-9-x-noAppearance br2  br-0 br--left  w-100 bn outline-0 bg-base c-on-base b--muted-4 hover-b--muted-3 t-body pl5 " autocomplete="off" placeholder="Encontre na Artwalk" type="text" id="downshift-0-input" value="">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header search input (#downshift-0-input) with the placeholder "Encontre na Artwalk". Its <label> is visually hidden, so the placeholder is the only visible text that identifies the field. The live style bundle sets .vtex-styleguide-9-x-input::placeholder to color:#8c8f94, makes the input background transparent, and gives the search bar's .vtex-input-prefix__group background-color:#eceded. That matches the colours Rampa measured: 2.77:1 at 14px and weight 400. On header hover (#f2f2f2) it is 2.90:1, and even on white it would be 3.24:1, all below 4.5:1. Placeholder text is visible text that conveys information, and no 1.4.3 exception (incidental, inactive control, logotype) applies, so it fails. The full-page screenshot shows the header band blank (the sticky header was not painted in that capture), but the measured colours match the live CSS, so that capture artefact does not touch this claim.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the header search field. Its placeholder "Encontre na Artwalk" is the only visible text in the field; the label "Buscar produtos" is the search button's aria-label and is not visible. The live theme stylesheet (overrides.css) sets .vtex-styleguide-9-x-input::placeholder to color #8c8f94, 14px, weight 400. The input background is transparent over .vtex-input-prefix__group, which is #eceded. That gives 2.77:1 (I recomputed it), below the 4.5:1 that normal-size text needs. In the hover state the group turns #f2f2f2, about 2.97:1, so that fails too. I checked the reasons a skeptic might raise. None of the 1.4.3 exceptions applies: the field is active, the text is not decorative, and it is not a logotype. The ACT rule and axe skip placeholders, but that is a gap in their scope; WCAG grants no exemption, and the placeholder carries the field's only visible cue. The live CSS and HTML match the capture, so the capture does not differ.
