ref: #id-k61aax > form > div > label > div > input
message: The field "Código postal" asks for the user's postal code but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="postal-code" is missing.

patch.ref: #id-k61aax > form > div > label > div > input
patch.before: <input class="vtex-styleguide-9-x-input ma0 border-box vtex-styleguide-9-x-hideDecorators vtex-styleguide-9-x-noAppearance br2   w-100 bn outline-0 bg-base c-on-base b--muted-4 hover-b--muted-3 t-body ph5 " placeholder="Código postal" type="text" value="">
patch.after: <input class="vtex-styleguide-9-x-input ma0 border-box vtex-styleguide-9-x-hideDecorators vtex-styleguide-9-x-noAppearance br2   w-100 bn outline-0 bg-base c-on-base b--muted-4 hover-b--muted-3 t-body ph5 " placeholder="Código postal" type="text" value="" autocomplete="postal-code">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Postal-code (CEP) text field in the 'Insira uma localizacao' delivery popover, placeholder 'Codigo postal', no autocomplete attribute. It collects the user's own delivery postal code, a purpose listed in 'Input Purposes' (postal-code), so 1.3.5 requires autocomplete='postal-code' (H98); without it the purpose is not programmatically determinable. The claim names that. The live SSR HTML renders the same input with no autocomplete.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: A text input in the delivery-location popover, placeholder 'Código postal', with no autocomplete attribute in the capture or in the live server HTML. The popover says offers and delivery vary by region, and the link beside it reads 'Não sei meu CEP' ('I don't know my CEP'), so the field asks for the user's own postal code. That is information about the user, and postal-code is one of the listed input purposes. Nothing else identifies the purpose programmatically, so it fails 1.3.5. The popover is hidden in the server HTML and opens client-side (it was open in the capture), but the same input is what users get when it opens.

ref: #email
message: The field "E-mail" asks for the user's email address but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="email" is missing. Chromium's own form check flags this field too.

patch.ref: #email
patch.before: <input class="lojaspompeia-lojaspompeiaio-2-x-NewsletterInputEmail" id="email" type="email" name="email" placeholder="seuemail@exemplo.com" value="">
patch.after: <input class="lojaspompeia-lojaspompeiaio-2-x-NewsletterInputEmail" id="email" type="email" name="email" placeholder="seuemail@exemplo.com" value="" autocomplete="email">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Newsletter e-mail field (label for=email 'E-mail', type=email, name=email) with no autocomplete attribute. It collects the user's own e-mail, a listed input purpose, so 1.3.5 needs autocomplete='email'; type=email gives the data type, not the purpose. The snapshot records Chromium's form issue FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError on it, so the second sentence also holds. The live NewsletterFormSection.min.js renders the input without autocomplete.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The newsletter 'E-mail' field: <input id='email' type='email' name='email' placeholder='seuemail@exemplo.com'> with no autocomplete attribute. It asks for the user's own email, which is in scope for 1.3.5 and on the input-purpose list. type='email' gives the data type, and name/id are not a programmatic purpose, so nothing satisfies H98 and the field fails 1.3.5. The snapshot records Chromium's form issue FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError on this input, so the second sentence of the claim is true too. The newsletter is client-rendered and shown in the screenshot.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: [visual context] Hidden SEO menu link (font-size 0, height 0, still exposed and focusable) to /feminino/fitness/plus-size. A second 'Moda Fitness' link in the same FEMININO sub-list goes to /moda-fitness-feminino. Both share name and context (parent list item FEMININO; the 'Categorias' and 'Plus Size' group labels are sibling items, not context; no title or heading). The destinations are not equivalent (all women's fitness vs. plus-size fitness only). The visible hover mega-menu puts them under different column titles ('Categorias' vs 'Plus Size'), so sighted users can tell them apart and AT users cannot: the pair fails 2.4.4 under R1, as the claim says. Live SSR HTML has the same menu.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: 'Moda Fitness' under the FEMININO > Plus Size group (/feminino/fitness/plus-size...). It shares its name and parent list item (FEMININO) with the 'Moda Fitness' under Categorias (/moda-fitness-feminino). Those are different listings (all women's fitness wear vs a plus-size filter), so they are not equivalent, and the claim holds of the capture. The link is in the 'seoMenuNav' copy of the menu. Live Menu.min.css gives .seoMenuItem/.seoSubMenuItem height:0 and .seoSubMenuLink font-size:0; line-height:0, so sighted users never see it, but it is in the accessibility tree and focusable. That copy is a flat list: the column labels ('Feminino', 'Masculino', 'Plus Size') are sibling list items, not headings, so by this rubric's context list the only context is the parent list item, which these same-name links share, and they lead to non-equivalent listings. Whether that fails 2.4.4 depends on R1's 'visual information' clause, and R1 does not cover links nobody can see. Read literally, nothing visible tells this pair apart, so the pair meets the expectation (no). But the visible mega-menu (hover-rendered; the CSS has SubMenuList/SubMenuBannerImg) very likely shows the same links under visible column titles. If so, the purpose is clear to sighted users and only assistive-technology users get the ambiguous copies, which is not 'ambiguous to users in general'. The capture has no hover state to confirm the visible dropdown. Competent auditors would split on this, so the label is uncertain.

html: <input class="vtex-styleguide-9-x-input ma0 border-box vtex-styleguide-9-x-hideDecorators vtex-styleguide-9-x-noAppearance br2   w-100 bn outline-0 bg-base c-on-base b--muted-4 hover-b--muted-3 t-body ph5 " placeholder="Código postal" type="text" value="">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Same postal-code input. It is wrapped in an empty <label> (only a div and the input inside), so Chrome takes the label as its name source and computes an empty name instead of falling back to the placeholder: the CDP node has role textbox, labelledby the label, and no name. Users of Chromium browsers get an unnamed edit field, so the name is not programmatically determined and 4.1.2 fails, as claimed (other engines may fall back to the placeholder, which does not cure it in Chrome/Edge). Live SSR markup is identical.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The postal-code input is wrapped in an empty <label> and has only placeholder='Código postal'. The capture's Chrome CDP tree gives it role textbox with no name, so the claim is true of the capture. The skeptic's point: HTML-AAM's input name computation says 'If the accessible name is still empty ... use the value of the control's placeholder attribute', and ACT rule e086e5 (Passed Example 5) treats a placeholder as enough for a non-empty accessible name. By the spec, the field's name is 'Código postal', and Chrome's empty result after the empty label looks like a user-agent quirk. Users of Chrome still get no name exposed. Whether that is an authoring failure of 4.1.2 is something competent auditors would disagree on. The live server HTML has the identical markup.

patch.ref: #input_3_1
patch.before: <input name="input_1" id="input_3_1" type="email" value="" class="large" tabindex="51" placeholder="Email address*" aria-required="true" aria-invalid="false">
patch.after: <input name="input_1" id="input_3_1" type="email" value="" class="large" tabindex="51" placeholder="Email address*" aria-required="true" aria-invalid="false" autocomplete="email">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the email field (#input_3_1, type="email", placeholder "Email address*") of the footer "Stay connected / Subscribe to our newsletter" sign-up form, so it collects the user's own email address, a purpose listed in WCAG's Input Purposes ("email"). claimTrue: the captured HTML has no autocomplete attribute, as the claim says. elementFails: type="email" only states the data format, not that the field asks for the user's own address; the sufficient technique for 1.3.5 is H98 (autocomplete="email"), which is absent, so the purpose is not programmatically determined. captureDiffers: the live HTML (curl) and the live DOM in Edge 158 show the same input with no autocomplete attribute, and the screenshot matches the live rendering. The claim names exactly this failure, so true positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the email field of the footer newsletter sign-up form (Gravity Forms, 'Stay connected / Subscribe to our newsletter'): <input type=email id=input_3_1 placeholder='Email address*'> whose associated label reads 'Email(Required)'. The claim is true of the capture: the field asks for the subscriber's own email address and has no autocomplete attribute. I looked for reasons it could pass. type=email does not cure it: Understanding 1.3.5 says type="email" indicates that the field is for an email address but does not clarify if the purpose is for entering the user's email address or some other person's email, and the only sufficient technique is H98 (autocomplete). The field is in scope: a newsletter sign-up collects the user's own address, and 'email' is in the Input Purposes list. No script adds the attribute: the snapshot is the post-script DOM and lacks it. The live HTML fetched today has the same input with no autocomplete (the only autocomplete values on the page are 'off' and 'new-password' elsewhere), so the capture does not differ. No reason against the finding holds up; the claim names the real failure.

ref: #input_3_1
subject: textbox
message: The browser exposes this element as a textbox but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "textbox", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).
html: <input name="input_1" id="input_3_1" type="email" value="" class="large" tabindex="51" placeholder="Email address*" aria-required="true" aria-invalid="false">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the same newsletter email field (#input_3_1). Its label <label for="input_3_1">Email(Required)</label> is hidden by the theme's CSS (main.css: .mailing-block .gfield_label{display:none !important}), and the only visible cue is the placeholder "Email address*". claimTrue: the snapshot's browser accessibility node gives role textbox with name "" (the label shows as notRendered), so the browser computed no name. elementFails: in Edge 158 (Chromium) on the live page, CDP gives the same empty name: the hidden label is taken as the name source with empty text, and the placeholder is marked superseded, so assistive technology gets no name in Chromium browsers. That is F68 (a control with no programmatically determined name); relying on a display:none label is not accessibility supported there, whatever other engines do. captureDiffers: the live page reproduces the hidden label, the empty computed name and the same visible field, so no difference touches the claim. "Announces only textbox" simplifies what is read (required state, maybe the placeholder), but the claim names the real failure, an empty accessible name, so true positive.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: Same email field. Its <label for=input_3_1> ('Email(Required)') is hidden by the theme (main.css: .mailing-block .gfield_label{display:none !important}). The snapshot records Chrome's own computation over CDP: role textbox, name "", labelledby the hidden label, which is ignored as notRendered. In Chromium a label that yields an empty string stops the name computation, so the placeholder 'Email address*' is not used as the name either. The first half of the claim, that the browser computes no name, is true of the capture. The live HTML and CSS fetched today match it, so the capture does not differ. Chrome's tree gives an empty name, which is F68's test ('using the browser's accessibility tree ... an accessible name that is neither empty nor composed solely of whitespace'), so I answer that the element fails there. The skeptic's reasons against it still hold up, though. AccName 1.2 step 2A keeps hidden content when it is part of a native label traversal whose root was hidden, so the hidden label names the control by the spec (Rampa's own computed name is 'Email(Required)'). Firefox and axe-style checks would get a name from the label or fall back to the placeholder. Screen readers commonly announce the placeholder, so 'announces only textbox' is probably overstated. Whether a spec-conformant hidden label plus a placeholder fails 4.1.2 because Chromium drops them is a point competent auditors would split on. Many would instead fail it under 3.3.2 or 2.5.3 for a label that only appears as a placeholder. Hence uncertain.

ref: #inputAddress
message: The field "My Address" asks for the user's street address but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="street-address" is missing.

patch.ref: #inputAddress
patch.before: <input type="text" class="form-control" id="inputAddress" name="inputAddress" placeholder="411 Legislative Ave, Dover, DE 19901">
patch.after: <input type="text" class="form-control" id="inputAddress" name="inputAddress" placeholder="411 Legislative Ave, Dover, DE 19901" autocomplete="street-address">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the text input #inputAddress, labelled "My Address" under "Find My Legislator", with the placeholder "411 Legislative Ave, Dover, DE 19901" and no autocomplete attribute in either the snapshot or the live HTML. It asks for the user's own address, which portal_ready.js sends to legis.delaware.gov/FindMyLegislator as the search term. That is information about the user, and the address is a purpose on the WCAG Input Purposes list (street-address and its parts). Without an autocomplete token the purpose cannot be programmatically determined, so the field fails 1.3.5 as the claim says. One nuance: a single field for the full address (street, city, state, ZIP) has no exact token, but street-address is the conventional mapping and does not change the outcome. The live markup matches the capture.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the single text input labelled 'My Address' in the Find My Legislator form. Its placeholder is '411 Legislative Ave, Dover, DE 19901', and portal_ready.js sends its value as one search string to legis.delaware.gov/FindMyLegislator. The claim holds of the capture: the field asks for the user's own address and has no autocomplete attribute, in the snapshot and in the live HTML alike. But the field takes a whole postal address in one input: street, city, state and ZIP. WCAG's Input Purposes list gives those as separate purposes (street-address, address-level2, address-level1, postal-code), and HTML autocomplete takes one field name per control. Understanding 1.3.5 says: 'If an input field accepts two different types of input purpose ... and the technology used does not allow multiple purpose values to be defined, it is valid to provide either one or the other value or leave out the designation of input purpose altogether.' So leaving out the designation is a valid way to meet 1.3.5 here. Requiring autocomplete="street-address" applies a stricter rule than the criterion; that token would also cover only the street part of what the field asks for. The live page matches the capture.

ref: html > body > footer > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(3) > a:nth-of-type(3) > img
subject: Trusted Information Creator Logo
message: The text alternative "Trusted Information Creator Logo" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.

patch.ref: html > body > footer > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(3) > a:nth-of-type(3) > img
patch.to: Award-winning information from the Patient Information Forum

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the third badge in the footer: the PIF TICK quality mark (image text 'Trusted Information Creator / Patient Information Forum'), the only content of a link to /prostate-information/further-help/our-award-winning-information, with alt 'Trusted Information Creator Logo' and no title. claimTrue: yes. The alt is all the link holds, and it names the badge, not the destination page, so the sentence holds of the capture. elementFails: no. Under H30/G82, the alternative read as the link text has to let users tell the link's purpose, and R2 accepts an alternative that names the destination's subject. The linked page (it now redirects to 'Help review our award-winning information') has a section, 'Our award-winning information', that matches the URL slug and explains that the PIF TICK 'is awarded to organisations who demonstrate they are trusted information creators' and that Prostate Cancer UK holds it. So a link named 'Trusted Information Creator' leads to the organisation's account of that accreditation, and its purpose can be determined from the name. Dropping 'Logo' and adding 'PIF' would be better practice but is not required by 1.1.1. captureDiffers: no. The live page's footer HTML has the same link, href and alt, and the screenshot shows the same three badges as the live page. The claim requires the alt to name the destination page itself, which is stricter than 1.1.1 requires.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the PIF TICK quality-mark badge (image text 'Trusted Information Creator / Patient Information Forum'), the only content of the third footer badge link, next to the Fundraising Regulator and Investing in Volunteers badge links. claimTrue: in the snapshot the img is all the link holds (link name 'Trusted Information Creator Logo', nameFrom contents, no title), and the alternative names the badge as a logo rather than stating a destination, so the sentence holds. captureDiffers: the live footer HTML fetched today is identical (same href, same img and alt) and the screenshot shows the badge row rendered normally; no difference touches the claim. elementFails: the href /prostate-information/further-help/our-award-winning-information redirects to 'Help review our award-winning information', whose section 'Our award-winning information' explains the PIF TICK, says it is awarded to 'trusted information creators', and shows this same logo. Read as link text in a row of accreditation badges, 'Trusted Information Creator' names the subject the link leads to (this accreditation), which by the rubric's R2 first test describes the purpose, so my lean is that it passes; the word 'Logo' describes the image but does not hide the subject. Against that, H30 asks the alternative to give the link's unique function, the landing page after the redirect opens with volunteer recruitment under a different title, and a user cannot tell it leads to the charity's own page rather than to the Patient Information Forum (as the two neighbouring badges lead to their accreditors). Competent auditors would reasonably disagree on whether a badge-name alternative suffices here, so the label is uncertain. Separately, the alternative omits 'Patient Information Forum' shown in the image, a text-equivalence point the claim does not raise.

ref: #mh-search
subject: Search
message: The text "Search" has at most 3.10:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ffffff on #009cdb), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (an element over or under it). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the 'Search' button of the myhome.ie property-search widget in the sidebar (#mh-search). claimTrue: the snapshot records white text (#ffffff, from CSS) on #009cdb, 13px bold, axe reason bgOverlap, 3.098:1; I sampled the screenshot inside the button's bounds and the dominant background is #009cdb with #ffffff glyphs, which computes to 3.10:1, so the sentence holds. elementFails: the live widget stylesheet (media.myhome.ie/cdn/widget/styles.css, loaded by the widget script the live article still embeds) sets #mh-search to background #009cdb !important, color #fff !important, font-weight bold; the text is 13px (at most 16px if it inherited the widget body size), bold, well under the 14pt (about 18.7px) bold threshold for large text, so 1.4.3 requires 4.5:1 and 3.10:1 fails; there is no image or gradient behind the text that could raise it. captureDiffers: the screenshot shows the styled page and widget as a browser renders it, and the live HTML and the widget's live CSS give the same colours and weight, so nothing in the capture differs in a way that touches this claim. The claim names exactly this failure, so true_positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the 'Search' button (button#mh-search) of the MyHome property search widget in the article's right sidebar. claimTrue: the snapshot records pixelContrast with axeReason bgOverlap, foreground #ffffff from CSS, background #009cdb (common, best and worst), 13px, weight 700, ratio 3.098; my own count of the screenshot pixels inside the button bounds gives #009cdb as the background (3693 px) and #ffffff as the glyph colour, so the sentence holds. elementFails: I looked for reasons it could pass and found none. The widget is injected on the live page by media.myhome.ie/cdn/widget/search-widget.js, whose stylesheet (media.myhome.ie/cdn/widget/styles.css) sets #mh-search { background: #009cdb !important; color: #fff !important; font-weight: bold !important }, so these are the colours users get, not a capture artefact; white on #009cdb is 3.10:1 by the WCAG luminance formula. The text is about 13px bold (it would be under the 18.66px bold large-text threshold even at the 16px the widget body sets), so 4.5:1 applies. The button is an active control, not disabled, not a logotype and not decorative, so no 1.4.3 exception applies; being third-party content does not exempt it from the page's conformance. captureDiffers: the live page (fetched today) embeds the same widget script, and its stylesheet's !important rules fix the same colours; the screenshot shows the styled layout, so nothing that differs touches this claim. Label true_positive: the button fails 1.4.3 for the low contrast the claim names.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The "Inscreva-se" button of the Gestão Financeira card in the "Graduação em um curto tempo" shelf; partly clipped by the carousel, label visible on the #ee325d fill. Measured: the snapshot's pixel measurement gives white text (#ffffff, from CSS) on #ee325d, 16px weight 500, 4.00:1; my own sampling of the screenshot within the button's bounds gives the same two colours (#ffffff glyphs on #ee325d fill), and the computed ratio is 4.00:1. 16px at weight 500 is not large-scale text (18pt, or 14pt bold), so 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1 and the button label fails. claimTrue yes: colours, ratio and the axe 'bgOverlap' reason are all as the snapshot records. captureDiffers no: the screenshot is a fully styled render; the live page's server HTML is client-rendered for these shelves, but its data still holds the same shelf and the current JS theme keeps SecondaryActionColorPure #EE325D, the same CTA style as the header button whose live CSS is background-color #EE325D, color #FFFFFF. The claim names the real failure, so true_positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the 'Inscreva-se' button of the Gestão Financeira card, the fourth card of the 'Graduação em um curto tempo' carousel; the carousel clips the card's right edge, but the button text is visible in the screenshot. I sampled the screenshot inside the button's bounds: the fill is #ee325d and the glyph pixels are #ffffff, 4.00:1, exactly what the message states. The text is 16px at weight 500, so it is not large text (24px, or 18.66px bold) and 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1; neither the logotype nor the incidental exception applies to an active enrol button. Reasons I looked for that would make it pass and did not find: the page carries a Perto Digital accessibility plugin, but the capture lists only voice assistant, Libras and face navigation, no contrast switch that would satisfy G174; the pink is not a hover or focus state but the resting style (every card button on the page has it). captureDiffers: the cards are rendered client-side, so the live server HTML I fetched does not hold them, but its __NEXT_DATA__ lists the same courses in the same order and its theme sets the action colour to #EE325D, and the header CTA's live CSS is background #EE325D with color #FFFFFF; the screenshot is a fully styled Chromium render, so nothing suggests users get other colours. The element fails 1.4.3 for the reason the claim gives.

subject: Pesquisar
message: The placeholder "Pesquisar" has a contrast of 4.17:1 with the field (#1212128f on #f5f5f5). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input aria-invalid="false" autocomplete="off" id=":r0:" placeholder="Pesquisar" type="text" class="MuiInputBase-input MuiOutlinedInput-input MuiInputBase-inputAdornedStart MuiInputBase-inputAdornedEnd MuiAutocomplete-input MuiAutocomplete-inputFocused emotion-css-1gnht4k" aria-autocomplete="list" aria-expanded="false" autocapitalize="none" spellcheck="false" role="combobox" value="">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The search combobox at the top of the page, whose only visible label is its placeholder "Pesquisar". The snapshot gives the placeholder colour #1212128f (≈56% #121212) on the field background #f5f5f5, 16px weight 500; my sampling of the screenshot finds the placeholder glyphs at #767676 on #f5f5f5, which is 4.17:1, below 4.5:1 for normal-size text. Understanding 1.4.3 (WCAG 2.1) states that the criterion "applies to text in the page, including placeholder text", and here the placeholder is also the field's only visible label, so the field fails 1.4.3. claimTrue yes. captureDiffers no: the screenshot is a styled render consistent with the snapshot; the live page still configures this search section with searchPlaceholder "Pesquisar" (the field itself is client-rendered, so my fetch could not redraw it, but nothing suggests a different style). true_positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the course search combobox under the 'Graduação' banner; its only label is the placeholder 'Pesquisar' (accessible name from placeholder, no visible label). In the screenshot the placeholder glyphs reach #767676 on a #f5f5f5 field, 4.17:1, which is #121212 at alpha 0x8f composited on #f5f5f5, as the message says. At 16px weight 500 it is not large text, so 4.5:1 applies. Reasons it could pass that I checked: 1.4.3's exceptions (inactive component, decoration, logotype) do not cover placeholder text in an active field, and the W3C WAI forms tutorial treats browser-default placeholder colours as not meeting WCAG's minimum contrast and shows how to style them to meet it, so placeholder text is text under 1.4.3; no contrast switch was found in the accessibility plugin. captureDiffers: the search field is rendered client-side and is absent from the live server HTML, so I could only compare the theme (same palette) and the styled Chromium render; nothing suggests a different placeholder colour for users. The element fails 1.4.3 for the reason the claim names.

subject: TRANSIÇÃO DE GOVERNO
message: The text "TRANSIÇÃO DE GOVERNO" has at most 4.09:1 contrast with what is behind it (#f5f5f5 on #0078db), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a pseudo-element). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the category tag 'TRANSICAO DE GOVERNO' on the first featured news card, a 12px, weight 400 Roboto label inside a blue pill over the photo. claimTrue: the snapshot gives computed colour rgb(245,245,245), 12px/400, background #0078db measured from pixels, 4.09:1, and records axe's reason as pseudo-content. elementFails: the live page's Elementor CSS sets the tag's inline-wrap background to var(--e-global-color-fc8d094) = #0078DB (opaque) and the text colour to var(--e-global-color-87f488d) = #F5F5F5; I compute 4.09:1 for that pair, under the 4.5:1 that 1.4.3 requires for text that is not large (12px normal weight). The tag is real informative text, not incidental or a logo. captureDiffers: the screenshot is styled and the live page still shows this card and tag with the same CSS. The claim names the failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the category badge 'TRANSIÇÃO DE GOVERNO' on the first featured news card (div.jet-listing-dynamic-field__content, 12px, weight 400). Claim: the snapshot gives the CSS colour rgb(245,245,245) and the screenshot pixels behind the text are #0078db (1676 of the sampled pixels); #f5f5f5 on #0078db computes to 4.09:1, so the sentence is true. Reasons I looked for: the live page's CSS sets the badge wrapper background to the global colour #0078DB and the text to #F5F5F5 at 12px (11px at a smaller breakpoint), the same as the capture, and the badge is still on the page, so the capture does not differ. The text is regular weight at 12px, so it is not large-scale text; it is a visible topic label, not decorative, incidental or a logotype. Even pure white text would reach only 4.46:1 on #0078db. The 'pseudo-element' note only explains why axe-core deferred; the background is a plain element background. The 'Alto Contraste' toolbar does not make it pass by G174, whose test requires the switched version to meet all other success criteria, which this page does not (for example, the radio button has no accessible name). It fails 1.4.3 at 4.09:1 against 4.5:1, as claimed.

ref: #player > button
subject: #player > button
message: The icon of this button has at most 1.61:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ffffff on #cccccc). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the Radio Roraima play button in the header: a 50x50 circle whose only content is a Font Awesome play glyph (aria-hidden); the 'Radio Roraima' h2 beside it is a separate element, not part of the control. claimTrue: the snapshot records the icon colour #ffffff from CSS and the circle #cccccc, 1.61:1, and the button shows nothing but the icon. elementFails: the live page's inline CSS sets .play-pause background-color #ccc and .play-pause i color #fff, so users get white on #ccc (1.61:1); the circle itself is also #ccc on the white header (1.61:1). The play glyph is the only visual cue of what the control does, so it is required to identify the component, and by G207's test (3:1 against the adjacent colour, the whole glyph is adjacent only to #ccc) it fails 1.4.11. captureDiffers: the screenshot is fully styled and the live HTML has the same markup and CSS for #player. The claim names exactly this failure. (Separately the button has no accessible name, a 4.1.2 issue.)

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the header radio player's play/pause button (button.play-pause, 50x50 circle), whose only content is a Font Awesome play glyph marked aria-hidden. Claim: the snapshot records the icon colour #ffffff from CSS on a #cccccc fill; my own pixel count of the screenshot gives #cccccc and #ffffff as the two dominant colours, 1.606:1, and the button holds no text, so the sentence is true of the capture. Reasons I looked for: (1) the live page's CSS is identical (.play-pause background-color #ccc, .play-pause i color #fff; :hover and :active keep #ccc; only the .paused state, reached after playing and pausing, turns the icon black), so the capture does not differ. (2) Adjacent text: the visible 'Rádio Roraima' is a separate h2 outside the button and names the station, not the action, so it does not convey what the play glyph conveys; Understanding 1.4.11 exempts graphics only when visible text gives the same information. (3) Boundary: the grey disc is itself 1.61:1 on the white header, so no part of the button reaches 3:1; the #8e8e8e pill outline (3.28:1) belongs to the container around the heading and does not show what the button does. (4) G174: the page has the pojo 'Alto Contraste' toolbar, which would restyle buttons, but G174's test requires the switched version to meet all success criteria and the switching control to conform, and this button has no accessible name in any presentation, so G174 does not hold. The play glyph is the only visual information that identifies the control's function and state, at 1.61:1 against the adjacent #cccccc, so it fails 1.4.11 (G207), as the claim says.

ref: #the_header > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > form > input
subject: Busca
message: The label "Busca" sits beside this field but is not tied to it: a screen reader announces the field only by its placeholder ("O que você procura?"), without the label.

patch.ref: #the_header > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > form > label
patch.before: <label for="s" class="sr-only">
patch.after: <label for="searchform" class="sr-only">

html:
<input id="searchform" style="background: none;" class="py-3 px-4 block w-full rounded-l border-none
            focus:z-10 focus:ring-0 dark:text-black" type="text" name="s" placeholder="O que você procura?" value="">

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header search field, input id="searchform" name="s" with the placeholder "O que você procura?". The capture has <label for="s" class="sr-only">Busca</label> as its DOM sibling. Because the label's for points to "s" while the field's id is "searchform", they are not associated, and the field's accessible name comes from the placeholder (nameFrom placeholder in the snapshot). So the claim is true of the capture: the label sits next to the field in the DOM, it is not tied to it, and the field is announced by its placeholder. The live HTML and the theme's .sr-only rule are the same, so the capture does not differ. The element still does not fail 1.3.1. The label is visually hidden: it is 1x1 px, shown: 0, and there is no "Busca" in the screenshot. So sighted users see no label-to-field relationship that could be missing from the code. What they do see is the placeholder and the magnifier button, and the placeholder is the field's programmatic name, which states that it is a search field. The text "Busca" is also there as text for assistive technology. The rule treated a hidden label that is not associated as a 1.3.1 failure, which is stricter than the criterion. A placeholder used as the only visible label is a matter for 3.3.2, not this claim.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the header search text field (id=searchform, name=s, placeholder 'O que você procura?'). The 'Busca' label next to it in the DOM is <label for="s" class="sr-only">: its for points at a non-existent id, so it is indeed not tied to the field, and the field's computed name comes from the placeholder; the sentence holds of the capture in DOM terms (claimTrue yes), though 'sits beside' suggests a visible label, which it is not. The snapshot records the label as 1x1 px with shown 0, the Tailwind sr-only class clips it, and the screenshot shows no 'Busca' text. 1.3.1 asks that information and relationships conveyed through presentation be programmatically determinable; a visually hidden label conveys no visual relationship, and the only visible cues (the placeholder text and the magnifier button) are exposed, the placeholder being the field's accessible name. F68, the failure for unassociated labels, is mapped to 4.1.2, not 1.3.1, and the field has a name there. So the field does not fail 1.3.1 for this reason; a placeholder-only visible label is at most a 3.3.2 question, which the claim does not raise. The live HTML matches the capture. The rule had the data showing the label is hidden and still reported it.

ref: #the_header > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > form > button
subject: #the_header > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > form > button
message: The icon of this button has at most 2.88:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#939598 on #fafafa). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).
html:
<button type="submit" class="inline-flex justify-center items-center h-auto w-16
        rounded-r font-semibold text-accent-500
        hover:bg-primary-500 hover:text-zinc-50 transition-all
        focus:z-10 focus:outline-none focus:ring-2 focus:ring-blue-500
    ">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header search form's submit button. It has no text and no accessible name, and it shows only a Font Awesome magnifier icon (fa-search). The button has no background or border of its own: it sits inside the form's #fafafa box, and the form's border goes around both the field and the button. The claim holds in the capture. I checked the screenshot pixels in the button's bounds: the solid icon pixels are #939598 on #fafafa, which is 2.877:1, and nothing else marks the control. On the live site, the theme's Tailwind CSS sets .text-accent-500 to rgb(147 149 152) and .bg-zinc-50 to rgb(250 250 250), and the live markup is the same as the capture, so the capture does not differ. The icon is the only visual information that identifies this control, so under 1.4.11 (G207, icons) it needs 3:1 against its neighbours. At 2.88:1 it fails, and the claim names that failure. The missing accessible name is a separate 4.1.2 problem.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the header search form's submit button, whose only visible content is a Font Awesome magnifier icon (class text-accent-500); it has no text and no own background or border. The theme's Tailwind CSS on the live site sets .text-accent-500 to rgb(147 149 152) = #939598 and the form's .bg-zinc-50 to rgb(250 250 250) = #fafafa; I recomputed the ratio as 2.88:1, below 3:1, so the claim is true of the capture and of the CSS (not an anti-aliasing artefact). The screenshot crop shows the same light-grey icon inside the near-white search box. Skeptic checks that did not hold up: the button is not inactive and its look is author-styled; the form's zinc-200 border only outlines the whole search box and does not show that a separate button exists, so the icon is the visual information required to identify the control (Understanding 1.4.11, G207); pressing Enter in the field is no exemption; the site's high-contrast toggle (accessibility.js adds a dark class) is not on by default and is not shown to be a fully conforming alternate version (the same pages share a non-descriptive title, for one). The live HTML and CSS match the capture, so captureDiffers is no. The claim names this failure.

ref: html
subject: Ministério Público do Estado do Acre
message: The page title "Ministério Público do Estado do Acre" says nothing about this page.
evidence: Ministério Público do Estado do Acre

patch.ref: html
patch.from: Ministério Público do Estado do Acre
patch.to: Ouvidoria-Geral | Ministério Público do Estado do Acre
patch.before: <title>Ministério Público do Estado do Acre</title>
patch.after: <title>Ouvidoria-Geral | Ministério Público do Estado do Acre</title>

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the document's title. The page is the Ouvidoria-Geral (ombudsman) page: its h1 and breadcrumb say "Ouvidoria-Geral". The captured title, set after scripts, is only the site name, "Ministério Público do Estado do Acre". I fetched the live page and it has the same <title>, so the capture does not differ. The home page, /atendimento-ao-cidadao/ and /transparencia/ return the same title too, so it is the same on every page. A site-wide title on a subpage does not describe this page's topic or purpose, as 2.4.2 and G88 require (see F25). A user with several tabs open, or a screen reader user arriving on the page, cannot tell from the title that this is the ombudsman page. The claim's "says nothing about this page" slightly overstates it, since the title does name the institution, but read in good faith it names the real failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The page is the Ouvidoria-Geral page (h1 'Ouvidoria-Geral', breadcrumb Início / Atendimento ao Cidadão / Ouvidoria-Geral), but its title is only the organisation's name, 'Ministério Público do Estado do Acre'. Fetching the live page, the home page and the Atendimento ao Cidadão page with curl returns that same <title> on all three, and the page has no script that rewrites document.title; the snapshot, taken in a browser after scripts ran, records the same title, so the capture does not differ. A title that is only the site name, shared by every templated page, does not identify this page's topic or purpose: that is F25 ('the title of a Web page not identifying the contents', whose example is a template site where all pages have the same title). No skeptic reason holds up: there is no other title source, and naming the site alone does not describe a subpage. The claim, read in good faith, names this failure.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The image is the green icon of the 'Oftalmologia' card in the 'Destaques' section: an eye chart of tumbling E letters over a trial frame, not a bicycle. It has alt="" in the capture and in the live HTML, and sits directly above the heading 'Oftalmologia' and the text about the ophthalmology emergency service, which already say everything it conveys. It is decorative and alt="" is correct under 1.1.1 (H67), so the element passes. The claim misdescribes the picture and wrongly says it conveys something the text does not; the model had the crop and the surrounding text and judged wrongly.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The Oftalmologia card icon (Icone_Oftalmologia_Site.svg, alt=""). The crop shows a green eye chart (rows of the letter E) above a trial frame for eye tests, not a bicycle. It sits directly above the h3 'Oftalmologia' and the text about the eye emergency service, so it only illustrates the topic the heading names and conveys nothing the text does not say. A null alt is correct for such a decorative or redundant image (H67), and the image is not inside a link. The claim is false of the capture: it is not a bicycle, and nothing is lost. The live page has the same markup. The model had the image and the heading and misjudged both.

skeptic.label: true_positive

patch.after: <a href="https://hjsc.com.br/japones/" class="menu-link" lang="ja">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The link text '日本語' (Japanese for 'Japanese language') is a Japanese phrase in a page whose html element is lang="pt-BR". Neither the snapshot's HTML nor the live HTML has a lang attribute on the link or any ancestor: the only lang attribute on the live page is pt-BR on html, and there is no hreflang. The word is not a proper name, a technical term or part of the Portuguese vernacular, so its language cannot be programmatically determined and a screen reader will voice it with the Portuguese voice. Fails 3.1.2 as the claim says (H58 is the remedy).

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Link '日本語' (to the Japanese-language page) on a page with html lang="pt-BR". The snapshot has no other lang attribute anywhere, and the live HTML has no lang="ja" either, so the Japanese text inherits pt-BR. Skeptic check on the 3.1.2 exceptions: it is a word in Japanese script, not a word of indeterminate language, not part of Portuguese vernacular, and a language's own name is not treated as a proper name here; Understanding 3.1.2's 'alternative language links' example is exactly this case and marks each language name with lang. The language of this phrase cannot be programmatically determined, so it fails 3.1.2 as the claim says.

message: The placeholder "Looking for..." has a contrast of 4.00:1 with the field (#00000080 on #ffffff). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The header search input's placeholder "Looking for...", 11px weight 300, visible in the header in the screenshot. The live theme style.css sets `.btLightSkin input[type="text"]::-webkit-input-placeholder { color: rgba(0,0,0,.5) }`, which renders as #7f7f7f on the white field; the screenshot's darkest glyph pixels are #7f7f7f on #ffffff, 4.00:1. Another finding (pixel-contrast) reports the same failure on the same input.

ref: #top > header > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > figure > a
subject: #top > header > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > figure > a
message: The icon of this link has at most 1.68:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#00e676 on #ffffff). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: A link in the header to WhatsApp (api.whatsapp.com) whose only content is the WhatsApp logo image (icone_whatsapp_sem_fundo, alt=""). The "Fale com a SBH:" figcaption sits outside the link. The screenshot pixels give the green glyph #00e676/#00e777 on white at 1.68:1, so the claim is true of the capture, and the live page has the same markup and image. Whether this fails 1.4.11 turns on the logo exemption. Understanding 1.4.11 says "Logos are exempted from contrast requirements" and, for a logo used as a link, only that authors "as a best practice" should consider a variant with enough contrast. It also says a low-contrast presentation chosen by the author, not mandated by brand guidelines, is not essential and so not exempt. WhatsApp's green mark is low-contrast on white even in its official colour, but monochrome variants exist. So one auditor would exempt it as a brand logo and another would fail it under G207. My lean is that it passes under the logo exemption, but competent auditors would reasonably disagree, so the label is uncertain. Separately, the link has no accessible name (empty alt, no aria-label or title), which fails 1.1.1, 2.4.4 and 4.1.2; this finding does not claim that.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: Header link to api.whatsapp.com whose only content is the WhatsApp logo image (alt=""), with the figcaption 'Fale com a SBH:' outside the link. claimTrue: the image (same file live) is a #00e777/#00e676 bubble with a white handset on a transparent background over the white header, 1.68:1 against the white, and it is all the link shows. elementFails: no. It is a brand logo (WhatsApp's), and Understanding 1.4.11 says 'Logos are exempted from contrast requirements' and, under the essential exception, that when such a graphic is the only visible content of a user interface component 'normatively the exemption "carries over" to the user interface component, authors are encouraged (but not required)' to add a contrasting cue. The author-choice clause applies to logos that 'normally have sufficient contrast'; WhatsApp's own brand green (#25D366) on white is about 1.98:1, so it does not. The claim applies G207's 3:1 where the criterion exempts the logo. Separately, the link has no accessible name (empty alt, no text), a failure of 1.1.1/2.4.4/4.1.2, not of 1.4.11. captureDiffers: no, the live HTML and image file are the same.

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(2) > session > div > article > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul > li:nth-of-type(5) > a > img
subject: mail icone
message: The text alternative "mail icone" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.

patch.ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(2) > session > div > article > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul > li:nth-of-type(5) > a > img

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The element is the envelope icon (alt 'mail icone') that is the only content of the fifth link in the share row under the byline (whatsapp icone, linkedin icone, Facebook icone, X icone, mail icone); the link is mailto:?subject=<article title>&body=<article URL>, i.e. 'share this article by e-mail'. The link has no title, and no visible or programmatic 'Compartilhar' label; the list item holds only the image. claimTrue: the alt is all the link holds and it names the icon ('mail icone'), not the share action. elementFails: by H30 the alternative of an image that is a link's only content should describe the link's function; 'mail icone' describes the picture and does not say it shares this article, so my reading is a 1.1.1 failure. But 'mail' does tell users the link opens an e-mail, and with the article's h1 before it some competent auditors would accept it as identifying a mailto link's purpose (R2's first test), so auditors would reasonably disagree; hence uncertain. captureDiffers: the live HTML has the same img and alt; there the href is Cloudflare's email-protection obfuscation, which its script decodes into the same mailto the snapshot holds, so users receive the same link. In the screenshot this desktop row is partly covered by a floating video ad, which does not touch the claim.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the last icon in the share row under the byline (desktop copy). The image mail.svg, alt "mail icone", is all a link holds whose href, after Cloudflare's email decoding, is mailto:?subject=<article title>&body=<article URL>. The link opens the user's mail program to send the article. With the image replaced by its alternative (the G82 and R2 test), the link reads "mail icone", which names where it goes: email. The extra word "icone" is noise, but it does not hide the purpose. The sibling links "whatsapp icone", "linkedin icone", "Facebook icone" and "X icone" follow the same pattern, and Rampa did not flag them. An alt like "Compartilhar por e-mail" would be better practice, but 1.1.1 asks only for a name that describes the control's purpose, and "mail" does that for a mailto link. The live HTML has the same img and alt. In the screenshot a floating video ad covers this icon, but that does not affect the alternative. The claim that the alt does not say where the link leads is wrong, and the model had the href and the sibling links to see it.

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(2) > session > div > article > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > img

message: The text alternative "icon search" names a label, not what the image conveys here.

patch.ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(2) > session > div > article > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > img

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is a static (non-link) img, logo_ai_laranja.svg, in the 'Converse com ...' block under the featured image; the crop and screenshot show it is an image of the orange text 'NEOFEED AI', completing the visible phrase 'Converse com NEOFEED AI' beside the 'Pergunte para NeoFeed AI' search field. Its alt is 'icon search', evidently copied from the search button's icon next to it. claimTrue: the snapshot alt is 'icon search', a generic label-like string that does not convey what the image shows. elementFails: the image carries text ('NeoFeed AI') and its alternative must serve the equivalent purpose; a screen reader user hears 'Converse com icon search', which is wrong and misleading, so 1.1.1 fails (G94; the text in the image is not in the alternative). The claim, read in good faith, names this: the alternative does not convey what the image conveys. captureDiffers: the live HTML fetched now has the same img and alt 'icon search', and the screenshot is the fully styled page.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the image logo_ai_laranja.svg after the paragraph "Converse com" in the NeoFeed AI block below the lead photo. The crop and the screenshot show it is the orange wordmark "NEOFEED AI", so the block reads "Converse com NEOFEED AI". Its alt is "icon search", apparently copied from the search button's icon next to it. I looked for reasons it could pass. The image is not decorative: the product name is only in the image, and the input placeholder "Pergunte para NeoFeed AI" is a separate control. Even if it were decorative, a non-null wrong alt fails under F39. The image is not inside a link or button that names it. The live HTML fetched today has the same img with alt="icon search", so the capture matches. The alternative gives a screen-reader user "Converse com icon search" instead of the product name, which fails 1.1.1 (F30, an alternative that is not an alternative). Read in good faith, the claim that the alt does not give what the image conveys names this failure.

ref: #mc4wp-form-1 > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > p:nth-of-type(2) > input
message: The field "Seu melhor e-mail" asks for the user's email address but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="email" is missing. Chromium's own form check flags this field too.

patch.ref: #mc4wp-form-1 > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > p:nth-of-type(2) > input
patch.before: <input type="email" name="EMAIL" placeholder="Seu melhor e-mail" class="email-news" required="">
patch.after: <input type="email" name="EMAIL" placeholder="Seu melhor e-mail" class="email-news" required="" autocomplete="email">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the newsletter sign-up field of the Mailchimp for WP form 'Receba o NeoFeed no seu e-mail': input type=email name=EMAIL placeholder 'Seu melhor e-mail' (your best e-mail), required, with no autocomplete attribute. claimTrue: the snapshot shows no autocomplete, and its formIssues record Chromium's FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError for this field, so both sentences hold. elementFails: the field collects the user's own e-mail address, which is the 'email' purpose in WCAG's Input Purposes list, and HTML supports autocomplete; type=email only gives the data format and does not identify it as the user's e-mail, and the sufficient technique H98 is not used, so 1.3.5 fails. The claim names exactly that. (The field also has no label other than its placeholder, a separate 3.3.2/4.1.2 matter, not judged here.) captureDiffers: the live HTML has the same input with no autocomplete, and the snapshot is the rendered DOM, so no script adds it.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the newsletter sign-up field <input type="email" name="EMAIL" placeholder="Seu melhor e-mail"> under "Receba o NeoFeed no seu e-mail" (Mailchimp for WP form). It asks for the user's own email address, which is the 'email' purpose in WCAG's Input Purposes list. It has no autocomplete attribute: none in the snapshot's rendered DOM, and none in the live HTML fetched today, where no script adds one. I checked possible ways it could pass. type="email" sets only the data format, not that the address is the user's own, and Understanding 1.3.5 names autocomplete (H98) as the way to meet the criterion in HTML. A form-level autocomplete cannot carry a purpose token, and the form has none anyway. The snapshot records Chromium's issue FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError on the field, so the claim's last sentence is also true. The field fails 1.3.5 for the reason the claim gives.

ref: #cookieconsent\:desc > p > strong > span
subject: We use our own and third-party cookies to improve site navigation, performance, and security, display ads, and obtain statistics. By clicking on “Proceed with all”, you agree to the storage of information for such purposes, and it is possible to adapt the use of cookies according to your preferences in “Personalize
message: The text "We use our own and third-party cookies to improve site navi…" has at most 4.35:1 contrast with what is behind it (#797979 on #ffffff), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (it partly covers other elements). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the text span of the cookie-consent banner message, inside strong, so 14px bold (the Securiti stylesheet fixes .cc-window at font-size 14px). The snapshot measured foreground #797979 on #ffffff; I confirmed #797979 pixels on the white banner in the screenshot crop, and the ratio computes to 4.35:1. Bold 14px is below the large-text threshold (14pt bold, about 18.7px), so 4.5:1 applies and the text fails 1.4.3. On the live site the banner colours come from the Securiti config (customTheme.popup.text #797979, popup.background #ffffff), identical in the pt-br and en configurations, so pt-BR visitors see the Portuguese message in the same failing colour and size. The capture missed the site's globals stylesheet (the header is unstyled in the screenshot), but that stylesheet has no rule for the cc-* banner classes and today is served with cross-origin-resource-policy: cross-origin; the language difference changes only the words. Neither touches this contrast, so the capture difference does not matter here. The claim names the real failure: true positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the span holding the cookie banner's message text (#cookieconsent:desc > p > strong > span). claimTrue: the snapshot records CSS colour #797979 on a #ffffff background, 14px at weight 700, axe reason elmPartiallyObscuring and a pixel measure of 4.353:1; #797979 on white computes to 4.35:1, as stated. Skeptic checks: 14px bold is not large-scale text (needs 18.66px bold or 24px), so 4.5:1 applies; the banner is real, visible content, not incidental or inactive; there is no gradient or image behind it. captureDiffers: the capture holds the English fallback text while visitors in Brazil get Portuguese, but on the live page (Edge, pt-BR and en-US) the same span has computed colour rgb(121,121,121), 14px, 700, on the banner's rgb(255,255,255) background with opacity 1, and the live screenshot shows grey bold text on white; the language difference does not touch this claim. elementFails: 4.35:1 is below 4.5:1 for normal-size text, so the text fails 1.4.3 on the page users receive, and the claim names exactly that failure.

ref: #cookieconsent\:desc > p
subject: unmarked|pt-BR|We use our own and third-party cookies to improve site navigation, performance, and security, display ads, and obtain statistics. By clicking on “Proceed with all”, you agree to the storage of information for such purposes, and it is possible to adapt the use of cookies according to your preferences in “Personalize
message: This passage has no lang attribute, so it is read as Brazilian Portuguese (pt-BR), but it is in English (en).
evidence: We use our own and third-party cookies to improve site navigation, performance, and security, display ads, and obtain statistics.

patch.ref: #cookieconsent\:desc > p

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The element is the message paragraph of the Securiti cookie-consent banner (div role=dialog, aria-label cookieconsent). In the snapshot the html element has lang="pt-BR", and neither the body, the dialog nor the paragraph carries a lang attribute, while the paragraph reads "We use our own and third-party cookies...", which is English: the claim is true of the capture. On the live site the banner text is chosen by the Securiti SDK from the browser's Accept-Language (it echoes it through app.securiti.ai/core/v1/utils/geo/location, then loads pt-br.json or en.json from cdn-prod.securiti.ai; tenant_default_language is pt-br). A browser that prefers pt-BR receives the Portuguese text "Utilizamos cookies próprios e de terceiros...", which matches the page language and passes 3.1.2; a browser that prefers English receives exactly the captured English text, and the SDK never sets a lang attribute (the en.json message HTML has none), so for those real visitors the passage fails 3.1.2 for the reason the claim gives. The capture holds the English variant because the capturing browser asked for English, which differs from what the site's pt-BR audience receives and matters for this claim. Since whether the element fails depends on the visitor's browser language, and competent auditors would reasonably disagree on whether the English variant of a pt-BR site counts as the page users receive, the label is uncertain.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the paragraph of the Securiti cookie-consent banner (#cookieconsent:desc > p). claimTrue: in the snapshot the paragraph is English text with no lang attribute on it or any ancestor, inside <html lang="pt-BR">, so the sentence holds for the capture. captureDiffers: the banner is injected by GTM (cookie-consent-sdk-loader.js), which first loads en.json as a default and then, once app.securiti.ai/core/v1/utils/geo/location answers, loads the location's language file. Loading the live page in Edge from the same location (Brazil) with locale pt-BR, and again with en-US, the banner settled in Portuguese both times (pt-br.json: "Utilizamos cookies próprios e de terceiros..."), with the same markup. Only when I blocked the geo request did it stay in English, with text identical to the capture (including the "Personalize / cookies" split). Rampa's capture also reports the page unsettled after 3000 ms and its main stylesheet failing, so it caught the SDK's interim fallback, not what a visitor receives. elementFails: on the page a person in Brazil receives the passage is Portuguese, the page's own language, so 3.1.2 does not apply and the element passes. Caveat: with a simulated US location the banner stays English and unmarked, which would fail 3.1.2 for visitors outside Brazil, but that is not the variant the capture's context serves. The claim rests on a capture artefact, so false positive, collector_error.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the 24x24 heart (wishlist) icon in the header. It is the only content of , which has no title or aria-label. Its alt is the full URL of the SVG file (whishlist-icon-lojasrede___....svg), and the snapshot computes the link's accessible name from that URL. claimTrue: the alt is a file URL, so it is a file name. elementFails: this is non-text content acting as a control, and its text alternative does not describe its purpose (wishlist / favourites). This is H30's failure and F30's (a file name used as the alternative), so it fails 1.1.1. captureDiffers: the live server-rendered HTML has the same inside the same link, with no title. The full-page screenshot leaves the fixed header blank, but the crop shows the heart icon, and that blank area does not affect the claim. Label: the claim names the failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the header wishlist icon (a heart, per the crop), the only content of a link to /account#/wishlist; its alt is the full asset URL '.../whishlist-icon-lojasrede___53704b35...svg', which becomes the link's name. The live server-rendered HTML fetched on 2026-11-25 has the same alt, and the link has no title, aria-label or other text in either (the CMS config has an 'attributeTitle' 'Wishlist Lojas Rede' that is not rendered), so the capture does not differ; the full-page screenshot shows the header area blank, a stitching artefact of the header that does not touch the alt. The only skeptic angle, that the URL contains 'whishlist-icon', does not cure it: F30 names file names as text alternatives that are not alternatives, and H30 requires the alternative of a link's only image to describe the link's function, which a long asset URL with a hash read aloud does not do. The element fails 1.1.1 and the claim names that failure.

ref: #newsletter-input-name
message: The field "Digite seu nome" asks for the user's first name but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="given-name" is missing.

patch.ref: #newsletter-input-name

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the name field of the footer newsletter sign-up form ('Cadastre seu e-mail e receba novidades...'): <input type="text" name="newsletter" id="newsletter-input-name">, labelled 'Digite seu nome', with no autocomplete attribute. claimTrue: the part about the missing autocomplete holds in the snapshot. Whether the field wants the first name ('given-name') or the full name ('name') cannot be told from 'Digite seu nome', since 'nome' can mean either. elementFails: the field collects the user's own name, an input purpose listed in WCAG 2.1 section 7, and nothing identifies that purpose programmatically (no autocomplete, so H98 is not met). It fails 1.3.5. captureDiffers: the server-rendered HTML of the live page (fetched 2026-11-25) has identical markup, also without autocomplete, so there is no difference that matters. Label: the claim names the real failure, a missing autocomplete that should identify the name purpose. The token it suggests may be 'name' rather than 'given-name', but that concerns the fix, not the failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive

subject: searchbox

ref: #accordion0
subject: Find out more about these del… | Why do scan reports matter? S…
message: None of the 2 tabs in this list is exposed as selected: a screen reader does not say which panel is open. Mark the current tab with aria-selected="true" (and the others with "false").
evidence: 2 tabs, none selected: Find out more about these del…, Why do scan reports matter? S…

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is an accordion of two items ("Find out more about these delays", "Why do scan reports matter?") that the site's accordion-js script turns into role=tablist, with each h3 header as role=tab carrying aria-expanded and each panel as role=tabpanel. In the capture both headers have aria-expanded="false", both panels are hidden (height 0), and the screenshot shows both items closed with a "Show more" button. claimTrue: no tab has aria-selected, as stated, but the rest of the sentence does not hold: no panel is open, and aria-expanded (a supported state of the tab role in ARIA 1.2) tells a screen reader that each item is collapsed, so it does convey which panel is open (none). elementFails: the state the user changes is open/closed; the script (updateARIA in vendor.min.js, read on the live site) sets aria-expanded to true or false on every toggle, and closes the other item (closeOthers), so the open/closed state can be programmatically determined and changes are exposed (ARIA5). Nothing is visually selected, so having no tab exposed as selected matches what sighted users see. The element meets 4.1.2 on this point. Requiring aria-selected on one tab applies the APG tabs pattern, a stricter rule than 4.1.2. Separately, putting role=tab on the h3 headers removes their heading role, which is a 1.3.1 concern, not this finding. captureDiffers: the live HTML has the same two items and text, and loads the same script that adds these roles. The capture was rendered with its styles, so nothing that differs touches this claim.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is an accordion of two collapsible sections ("Find out more about these delays", "Why do scan reports matter?"). In the server HTML these are plain h3 headers with tabindex=0; the theme's accordion-js script (vendor.min.js, read on the live site) adds role=tablist to the container, role=tab plus aria-expanded="false" to each header, and role=tabpanel to each content div. Its updateARIA function sets aria-expanded to true on the header whose section opens and back to false when it closes, and closeOthers (the default, not overridden) keeps at most one open. claimTrue: the first half holds, since neither tab has aria-selected. The second half does not: the snapshot's accessibility tree exposes expanded: false on both tabs, and in the capture no panel is open at all (both panels are hidden, matching the screenshot). So a screen reader does report the open or closed state, and once a section opens it says which one through aria-expanded. elementFails: 4.1.2 asks that states the user can set be programmatically determinable. The state the user sets here is expanded or collapsed, and it is exposed and kept up to date with aria-expanded, which is technique ARIA5. ARIA 1.2 lists aria-expanded as supported on tab and does not require aria-selected (it is a SHOULD for real tab widgets, and its implicit value is false). With zero or one section open, "none selected" matches the actual state, and no documented 4.1.2 failure covers a missing aria-selected. Requiring it applies a stricter ARIA-pattern rule than the criterion. Label false_positive, cause criterion_misapplied.
