The live choice.js theme for this site sets uxLinkColor #b71c1c and uxBackgroundColor #222222. The screenshot's banner pixels are #222222 with the glyphs peaking at #b71c1c. That is 2.42:1, well under 4.5:1. I looked for reasons it might pass: wrong pixel sampling, an overlay, or different colours on the live banner. None holds, because the CSS values match the pixels. The banner is part of the page that users in Ireland and the EU receive, and no partial-conformance statement excludes it. claimTrue: yes. captureDiffers: no. The failure is as the claim states.

ref: #subnav > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > nav > ul > li:nth-of-type(11) > span > button
subject: dropdown button
message: The icon of this button ("dropdown button") has at most 2.78:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#9b9b9b on #ffffff). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).
html: <button x-on:click="onClickSubNav !== 1 ? onClickSubNav = 1 : onClickSubNav = null" aria-label="dropdown button">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the caret button (aria-label "dropdown button") next to the "Services" text in the sticky main menu. The "Services" span toggles the same submenu but sits outside the button, so the caret is the only thing this button shows. claimTrue: the snapshot's pixel measurement gives #9b9b9b on #ffffff, 2.78:1. elementFails: the live arrow-drop.svg hard-codes the path fill as #9B9B9B, which overrides the svg's fill-current. The subnav background is white (bg-white), so users see 2.78:1, below 3:1. Understanding 1.4.11 (Figure 36) says such a down-arrow "is required to understand that there is drop-down functionality". That makes it required visual information, and it fails. captureDiffers: the full-page screenshot leaves the sticky subnav strip blank (it also omits the fixed consent dialog), so it looks like a screenshot artefact. The snapshot and the live HTML have the same markup and icon, so nothing differs that touches this claim. The claim names the real failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the icon-only 'dropdown button' next to 'Services' in the sticky main menu (#subnav). It has no text and no border, so the caret is all the button shows. The live sprite arrow-drop.svg hard-codes the path fill as #9B9B9B, which overrides the button's currentColor, and #subnav is bg-white. #9b9b9b on #ffffff is 2.78:1, below 3:1. The snapshot's pixel measurement and the dimmed nav in the stitched screenshot agree. I looked for reasons it might pass. The adjacent black 'Services' text names the menu, but it does not show that the menu drops down. Understanding 1.4.11 (Figure 36, dropdown indicator) says 'The down-arrow is required to understand that there is drop-down functionality'. The caret also rotates to show the expanded state. claimTrue: yes. captureDiffers: no. The top of the full-page screenshot is blank where the sticky nav belongs (a stitching artefact), but the live HTML and SVG give the same colours. The failure the claim names holds, so this is a true positive.

ref: #header-search
subject: Search for waterproof shoes...
message: The placeholder "Search for waterproof shoes..." has a contrast of 2.35:1 with the field (#00568080 on #e6eef2). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input id="header-search" class="search__input w-full input js-search-input" type="search" role="combobox" name="q" placeholder="Search for sun hats" autocomplete="off">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the same header search field, and the finding is about its placeholder text. The capture records the placeholder colour as #00568080 (the text colour at 50% opacity) on the field background #e6eef2, at 16px and weight 400. Blending gives about #73a2b9 on #e6eef2, which works out to 2.35:1, so the claim's figures are right. On the live page the computed ::placeholder colour is rgba(0,86,127,0.5) on rgb(230,238,242), also at 16px/400. That is the same ratio, and my crop of the live header shows the pale grey-blue prompt ("Search for sun hats...") on a pale field. So captureDiffers is no. The full-page screenshot leaves the sticky header blank, but the measurement came from the rendered field and matches the live page. The text is normal size, so it needs 4.5:1. Understanding 1.4.3 says the criterion applies to "text in the page, including placeholder text". This placeholder is also the only visible text that tells users what the field is for, because the label is display:none. At 2.35:1 it fails 1.4.3, which is the failure the claim names, so the label is true_positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the same header search field, and the finding is about the contrast of its placeholder. claimTrue: the snapshot's pixelContrast record gives the placeholder "Search for waterproof shoes..." (one of the strings in the field's data-placeholder attributes, which a script cycles through) at #005680 with 50% alpha on #e6eef2, 16px weight 400. Compositing gives about rgb(115,162,185), and I recomputed 2.354:1. elementFails: the live main.css sets .search__input::placeholder to rgba(var(--text-color)/.5), and the header style block sets --text-color: 0 86 127 and --search-bg-color: #e6eef2. That is the same 2.35:1, far below 4.5:1 for 16px normal text. When the search is open, the background turns white, and that still fails. On the 1280px desktop layout the field is visible: it collapses only below 769px, and its captured bounds are 350x44. I looked for reasons it could pass and found none. Placeholder text is text, and it is not inactive, decorative, invisible or part of a picture, so no 1.4.3 exception applies. Because the colour is semi-transparent, the measured background governs, and the live CSS confirms that background. captureDiffers: the full-page screenshot shows the header area blank, probably because of the sticky header. The measurement does not depend on it, though: the foreground came from CSS, and the live CSS has the same colours as the capture. So no difference touches this claim.

ref: #header-search
subject: combobox
message: The browser exposes this element as a combobox but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "combobox", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).
html: <input id="header-search" class="search__input w-full input js-search-input" type="search" role="combobox" name="q" placeholder="Search for sun hats" autocomplete="off">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header search field (input type=search, role=combobox, id=header-search). It has an explicit <label for=header-search>Search</label> with the class visually-hidden, but a page style sheet sets .visually-hidden{display:none}, so the label is not rendered. In the snapshot the browser's AX node is a combobox with name "", it lists the label as its labelledby relation, and the label's AX node is ignored as notRendered, so the claim that the browser computes no name is true of the capture. I loaded the live page in headless Edge (Chromium) through CDP at 1280x800. The label's computed display is none and the computed name is empty: the labelfor source gives "", and Chromium marks the placeholder (an animated typing prompt such as "Search for sun hats...") as superseded, so it does not supply the name. That is the same state as the capture, so captureDiffers is no. My fetch was also automated, but the rule comes from the page's own style sheet and scripts, which an ordinary browser runs too. A form field whose accessible name is empty fails 4.1.2, as the ACT rule e086e5 (form field has non-empty accessible name, which applies to combobox) expects. Some screen readers may still read the placeholder as a hint, but no name is exposed. The claim names exactly this failure, so the label is true_positive. The missing name also bears on 1.3.1 and 3.3.2.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the header search field, <input type=search role=combobox id=header-search>, preceded in the same form by <label class="label visually-hidden" for="header-search">Search</label>. claimTrue: in the capture the browser's accessibility tree (CDP) gives the combobox the name "" and marks that label ignored as notRendered, even though it lists the label as the labelledby relation, so the sentence is true of the capture. elementFails: the live HTML has the same label, and the live main.css defines .visually-hidden as the standard clip pattern (position:absolute; 1px by 1px; overflow:hidden; clip:rect(0,0,0,0)). No theme or app style sheet sets display:none on it, and no theme script touches it. That label keeps its layout box, so browsers name the field "Search" from the explicit label (H44). Rampa's own snapshot also computed "Search". The field has a name, so 4.1.2 is met. captureDiffers: across the whole capture, every .visually-hidden element lost its layout box. The skip link has no accessibility node, "SHOP ALL" links lost their hidden suffixes, and the search and carousel buttons got empty names. The CSS served today does not produce that state, so the empty name comes from the capture, not from the page users receive. I could not render the page in a browser myself; this rests on the served HTML and CSS. The cause is collector_error because the rule acted on the browser name from that capture.

ref: #shopify-section-template--33381603803461__section_collection_list_qE489T > ul > li:nth-of-type(1) > figure > picture > img
subject: Single Bed Mattress
message: The text alternative "Single Bed Mattress" describes something the image does not show.

patch.ref: #shopify-section-template--33381603803461__section_collection_list_qE489T > ul > li:nth-of-type(1) > figure > picture > img

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the first image in the "Mattresses by Size" list, alt="Single Bed Mattress", and it is not inside a link. The crop and the screenshot show a line icon of a single bed or mattress with a pillow, marked 3'. That is exactly what the alternative says, so the claim that it describes something the image does not show is false. The alternative is accurate and equivalent (the 3ft size is also in the heading link below), so 1.1.1 is met. The live HTML has the same image and alt. The model had the crop and the alt, and it judged wrongly.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the first tile image in the "Mattresses by Size" list (alt="Single Bed Mattress"). It is not a link; the h5 link "Single Bed Mattresses (3ft)" follows it. The crop shows a line icon of a narrow single bed with a pillow and the marking 3'. claimTrue: no; the alternative names exactly what the picture shows, a single bed mattress, so it does not describe something absent. elementFails: no; the alternative conveys the picture's information, and the 3ft size is also in the adjacent heading. At most the alternative is redundant with that heading, which is advisory, not a 1.1.1 failure. captureDiffers: no; the live HTML has the same img with the same alt in the same figure. The checker had the image and the alt and misjudged their match.

ref: #shopify-section-template--33381603803461__3e07fbd0-f156-4586-9767-b3171364d76c > div > article > figure > picture:nth-of-type(2) > img
subject: hidden home-page-banner-bedtime-img-v3.png
message: This image is hidden from screen readers (alt=""), but it conveys what the text around it does not say: "BEDTIME JUST GOT A WHOLE LOT BETTER, Dream - Worthy Mattress Collection".
evidence: BEDTIME JUST GOT A WHOLE LOT BETTER, Dream - Worthy Mattress Collection

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the desktop hero banner image (home-page-banner-bedtime-img-v3.png) with alt="". The crop shows text baked into the picture: "BEDTIME JUST GOT A WHOLE LOT BETTER" and "Discover our Dream - Worthy Mattress Collection". In the snapshot the sibling title div is empty, and that text appears nowhere else on the page, so the claim is true of the capture (it drops "Discover our", which does not matter). An image of text that carries a promotional message is not pure decoration, so its text alternative has to give that text. With alt="" screen reader users miss it, which fails 1.1.1. The live HTML has the same markup (alt="", empty title-styling div, no text copy), so the capture does not differ. The discount pop-up covers the banner in the screenshot, but that has no bearing on this claim.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the desktop hero banner image (picture.mobile-hide > img, alt="") at the top of the collection page; the crop shows the image of text "BEDTIME JUST GOT A WHOLE LOT BETTER / Discover our Dream - Worthy Mattress Collection" beside a photo of a woman hugging a pillow. claimTrue: the snapshot gives alt="" (Chrome ignores it as emptyAlt), the article's title-styling div is empty, the banner is not a link, and that wording appears nowhere else in the page (the h1 is just "Mattresses"); the quote drops "Discover our" but points at the right text. elementFails: I looked for a reason it passes: no caption, no overlay text, no figcaption, no aria-describedby, no adjacent copy repeating the slogan. Promotional copy is information, not pure decoration, so an image of text that carries it with a null alternative is F39 under 1.1.1. A reading that the slogan is mere decoration does not hold up, since the text is the banner's whole message. captureDiffers: the live HTML fetched on 2026-11-25 has the same two pictures with alt="" and the same empty title div; the newsletter pop-up that covers the screenshot's top also appears for real users and is dismissible, so it does not change this claim.

ref: #max
message: Nothing on screen tells what to enter in the field "to": its label is on the page, but its text does not show: the label looks the same with its text made transparent.

patch.ref: #max
patch.before: <input type="number" id="max" name="filter.v.price.lte" value="1349" max="1349">
patch.after: <label for="max">to</label> <input type="number" id="max" name="filter.v.price.lte" value="1349" max="1349">

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the maximum price field input#max in the Price filter, labelled by <label for="max">to</label>. The claim says the label's text does not show. The screenshot clearly shows "to" rendered between the "€ 0" and "€ 1349" fields, under the visible "Price" heading and range slider. The live CSS (.input-range>span label{display:block;position:absolute;right:100%;...;text-align:center}) places the label text there, and only the first label ("From") is moved off screen. So the claim is false of the capture. With "Price", the euro prefix and "to", the field's purpose is visible and clear, so it meets 3.3.2. The claim rests on the snapshot's textVisible=false flag for this label, which is wrong, so this is a collector error. The live page matches the capture.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the upper price filter field (input type=number #max, value 1349) with <label for="max">to</label>. The claim says the label's text does not show. The snapshot places the label at x 112.5-162.5, y 1853.7-1903.9, and the capture's own screenshot shows "to" in exactly that box, between the "€ 0" and "€ 1349" fields under the "Price" heading. The live screen.css styles ".input-range>span label" as display:block with normal text (no transparency), so the label is visible to users. claimTrue: no; the label's text shows in the screenshot. elementFails: no. Visually, "Price" + "€ 0" + "to" + "€ 1349" makes clear what to enter, which meets 3.3.2 for this field. (The lower field #min has its "From" label moved off screen, but that is another element.) captureDiffers: no; the live HTML and CSS match the capture. Cause: the collector's textVisible=false flag on this label is wrong, likely because the fixed newsletter pop-up overlay covered the viewport when the transparency test ran. The finding rests on that wrong data.

ref: #search_main
subject: searchbox
message: The browser exposes this element as a searchbox but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "searchbox", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).
html: <input type="search" id="search_main" name="q" placeholder="What are you looking for?" autocomplete="off" required="">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header search field input#search_main (type=search, placeholder "What are you looking for?"). Its only label is <label for="search_main">Search</label>, which the live screen.css hides with "#search label{display:none}". Chromium's accessibility tree in the capture gives the searchbox an empty name, with the hidden label as its labelledby source and no fallback to the placeholder, so the claim is true. In Chrome and Edge, which are ordinary browsers, assistive technology therefore gets a searchbox with no name: the legend "Search" only names the group, and the submit button is labelled "Zoeken". That fails 4.1.2. Firefox and the HTML-AAM order would fall back to the placeholder, which is a browser difference the fix should still cover (for example by visually hiding the label instead of using display:none). The live HTML and CSS match the capture.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the header search field (input type=search #search_main, placeholder "What are you looking for?") with <label for="search_main">Search</label> and a legend "Search". claimTrue: the snapshot's CDP tree gives the searchbox name "" with a labelledby relation to the label, and the label is ignored as notRendered, so Chrome computed no name, as the claim says (Rampa's own name "Search" differs from the browser's). captureDiffers: the live HTML has the same markup, and the live screen.css has "#search label{display:none}", so users receive the same display:none label. elementFails: in Chromium browsers the field reaches the accessibility API with an empty name, which is F68's failure, so I answer yes for what most users receive. But concrete reasons against hold up enough for competent auditors to split. By HTML-AAM the placeholder is the fallback name when the label yields nothing, and Firefox computes the placeholder (or the hidden label) as the name. Chrome itself exposes the placeholder as the description, so screen readers will likely still announce "What are you looking for?", which makes the claim's "announces only searchbox" doubtful in practice. Spec- or axe-based testing would likely pass it, while inspection of Chrome's tree would fail it. Hence uncertain.
